💻 Production-Ready Automation Code 1. Auto Stop Function (dc-common-lambda-auto-stop / lambda_function.py): import boto3 import os import json import logging import urllib3 from botocore.exceptions import ClientError logger = logging.getLogger() logger.setLevel(logging.INFO) ec2_resource = boto3.resource('ec2') http = urllib3.PoolManager() webhook_url = "https://hooks.slack.com/services/YOUR_WORKSPACE_ID/YOUR_CHANNEL_ID/YOUR_SECRET_TOKEN" def lambda_handler(event, context): environment_auto = os.environ.get('environment_auto') if not environment_auto: logger.info('Target environment tag is empty') return { "statusCode": 400, "body": "Environment variable 'environment_auto' is not set" } # RESILIENT FILTER: Only query instances with the target tag THAT ARE CURRENTLY RUNNING instances = ec2_resource.instances.filter( Filters=[ {'Name': 'tag:environment_auto', 'Values': [environment_auto]}, {'Name': 'instance-state-name', 'Values': ['running']} ] ) instance_list = list(instances) if not instance_list: logger.info("No running instances found to stop.") return { "statusCode": 200, "body": "No running instances found to stop (Instances already stopped or none exist)." } try: action_stop = instances.stop() send_slack(action_stop) return { "statusCode": 200, "body": f"EC2 Stopping successfully. Processed {len(instance_list)} instance(s)." } except ClientError as e: logger.error(f"Error stopping instances: {e}") return { "statusCode": 500, "body": str(e) } def send_slack(action_stop): try: list_instance_id = [] if ( len(action_stop) > 0 and "StoppingInstances" in action_stop[0] and len(action_stop[0]["StoppingInstances"]) > 0 ): for instance in action_stop[0]["StoppingInstances"]: list_instance_id.append(instance["InstanceId"]) msg = f"Stopping Instances ID:\n {list_instance_id}" data = {"text": msg} http.request( "POST", webhook_url, body=json.dumps(data).encode("utf-8"), headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"} ) logger.info("Sent stopping notification to Slack successfully") else: logger.info('No stopped instances to notify') except Exception as e: logger.warning(f"Error sending alert to Slack: {e}") 2. Auto Start Function (dc-common-lambda-auto-start / lambda_function.py): import boto3 import os import json import logging import urllib3 from botocore.exceptions import ClientError logger = logging.getLogger() logger.setLevel(logging.INFO) ec2_resource = boto3.resource('ec2') http = urllib3.PoolManager() webhook_url = "https://hooks.slack.com/services/YOUR_WORKSPACE_ID/YOUR_CHANNEL_ID/YOUR_SECRET_TOKEN" def lambda_handler(event, context): environment_auto = os.environ.get('environment_auto') if not environment_auto: logger.info('Target environment tag is empty') return { "statusCode": 400, "body": "Environment variable 'environment_auto' is not set" } # RESILIENT FILTER: Only query instances with the target tag THAT ARE CURRENTLY STOPPED instances = ec2_resource.instances.filter( Filters=[ {'Name': 'tag:environment_auto', 'Values': [environment_auto]}, {'Name': 'instance-state-name', 'Values': ['stopped']} ] ) instance_list = list(instances) if not instance_list: logger.info("No stopped instances found to start.") return { "statusCode": 200, "body": "No stopped instances found to start (Instances already running or none exist)." } try: action_start = instances.start() send_slack(action_start) return { "statusCode": 200, "body": f"EC2 Starting successfully. Processed {len(instance_list)} instance(s)." } except ClientError as e: logger.error(f"Error starting instances: {e}") return { "statusCode": 500, "body": str(e) } def send_slack(action_start): try: list_instance_id = [] if ( len(action_start) > 0 and "StartingInstances" in action_start[0] and len(action_start[0]["StartingInstances"]) > 0 ): for instance in action_start[0]["StartingInstances"]: list_instance_id.append(instance["InstanceId"]) msg = f"Starting Instances ID:\n {list_instance_id}" data = {"text": msg} http.request( "POST", webhook_url, body=json.dumps(data).encode("utf-8"), headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"} ) logger.info("Sent starting notification to Slack successfully") else: logger.info('No started instances to notify') except Exception as e: logger.warning(f"Error sending alert to Slack: {e}") 🛠️ Real-World Troubleshooting Bank 1. Invalid Instance State Exception (IncorrectInstanceState) Symptom: Calling start() raises: ClientError: An error occurred (IncorrectInstanceState) when calling the StartInstances operation: The instance is not in a state from which it can be started. Root Cause: EC2 instances can only transition to running from stopped. Attempting to start an instance that is already running, pending, or stopping triggers API rejection. Resolution: Incorporate state filters ({'Name': 'instance-state-name', 'Values': ['stopped']}) ensuring start actions are only executed against halted instances. 2. Ghost Terminated Instances Crashing Automation Symptom: Terminated instances previously tagged with environment_auto = true continue to trigger batch API failures. Root Cause: AWS retains metadata for terminated instances in the EC2 registry for several hours post-termination. Blanket tag queries inadvertently capture these dead resources. Resolution: Explicitly filter out terminated and shutting-down states, or target specific instance IDs directly. 3. Missing Security Group Visibility During Instance Launch Symptom: Security Group lambda-lab is absent from the selection dropdown in Step 2.3. Root Cause: Security groups are strictly VPC-scoped. The launch wizard defaults to the Default VPC, hiding security groups that belong to the custom lambda-lab VPC. Resolution: Select Edit under Network settings, switch the VPC selector from Default VPC to lambda-lab, and the custom security group immediately becomes selectable. 4. Premature Lambda Execution Timeout (Task timed out after 3.00 seconds) Symptom: Function invocation fails abruptly with CloudWatch log entry: Task timed out after 3.00 seconds. Root Cause: AWS Lambda defaults to a 3-second execution cap. Performing Boto3 instance queries combined with external HTTPS Slack webhook dispatch routinely requires 3.5 to 5 seconds. Resolution: Navigate to Configuration ➔ General configuration ➔ Edit, and elevate the Timeout parameter from 3 sec to 1 min. 5. Empty Target Collection Error (Target Instance is None - StatusCode 500) Symptom: Execution returns {"statusCode": 500, "body": "Target Instance is None"}. Root Cause: The Lambda tag filter found no matching resources. Common culprits include untagged compute, typos in the key (e.g., Environment_auto), trailing whitespace, or casing mismatches (True vs true). Resolution: Inspect EC2 tags to ensure exact lowercase matching: Key = environment_auto, Value = true. 6. Missing Environment Variable Configuration (StatusCode 400) Symptom: Function terminates early with Environment variable 'environment_auto' is not set. Root Cause: The environment_auto environment variable was omitted during Lambda configuration. Resolution: Add Key environment_auto with Value true under Configuration ➔ Environment variables. 7. Uncommitted Code Deployment Oversight Symptom: Modifying code in the editor has no effect during subsequent Test invocations. Root Cause: AWS Lambda requires an explicit Deploy action to update the $LATEST published version. Unsaved code remains in draft state. Resolution: Always select the orange Deploy button and wait for confirmation before testing. 8. Execution Role Permission Denial (UnauthorizedOperation) Symptom: Invocation crashes with ClientError: UnauthorizedOperation: You are not authorized to perform this operation. Root Cause: The function was deployed using the default Lambda basic execution role instead of the designated dc-common-lambda-role granting AmazonEC2FullAccess. Resolution: Update execution role binding under Configuration ➔ Permissions to assign dc-common-lambda-role. 9. Unhandled ChatOps Transport Exceptions Symptom: EC2 power operations execute successfully, but the entire Lambda function reports failure. Root Cause: Unhandled network timeouts or invalid Slack webhook endpoints raise unhandled exceptions during http.request(). Resolution: Encapsulate Slack dispatch within try...except Exception blocks, ensuring chat transport issues do not fail primary compute lifecycle operations. 10. EventBridge Scheduler Timezone Misalignment (UTC vs Local Time) Symptom: Power events trigger 7 hours off-schedule relative to local business hours. Root Cause: EventBridge Scheduler defaults to UTC+0, while local business hours operate under UTC+7 (Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh). Resolution: Explicitly declare the timezone as Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh or calculate the appropriate UTC offset when defining Cron expressions. 🧹 Resource Teardown Workflow To prevent unnecessary charges and protect account credits, decommission resources in the following dependency order:
Delete EventBridge Schedules: Navigate to Amazon EventBridge ➔ Schedules and delete both dc-common-lambda-auto-stop and dc-common-lambda-auto-start. Delete Lambda Functions: Navigate to AWS Lambda ➔ Functions and remove both deployed functions. Terminate Amazon EC2 Compute: Navigate to Amazon EC2 ➔ Instances, select lambda-lab-instance, and select Instance state ➔ Terminate instance. Delete Key Pair: Navigate to EC2 ➔ Key Pairs and delete lambda-lab-key. Delete Security Group: Once EC2 transitions to Terminated, navigate to VPC ➔ Security Groups and delete lambda-lab. Delete VPC lambda-lab: Navigate to VPC ➔ Your VPCs, select lambda-lab, and select Actions ➔ Delete VPC. Delete IAM Execution Role: Navigate to IAM ➔ Roles and delete dc-common-lambda-role.

title: Command Line Operations with AWS CLI
content:
The Command Line Operations with AWS CLI workshop was conducted on Tuesday (13/10/2026) as part of Week 5. This page records the authentic step-by-step walkthrough: exact console clicks, specific parameter inputs, shell commands executed, and resolution of encountered technical issues. 🔗 Workshop Reference: Getting Started with the AWS CLI
🎯 Lab Objectives: Establish a standard practice environment using IAM User Groups, IAM Users (aws-cli-user, devops), and generated CLI Access Keys. Launch an Amazon EC2 Management Instance (Amazon Linux 2023) workstation and establish secure remote access via MobaXterm. Install the latest version of AWS CLI v2 in a Linux environment and configure multiple profiles (default, devops). Use AWS CLI to manage object storage on Amazon S3 (bucket creation, file upload, object listing, and safe deletion using the --force flag). Administer notification messaging services using Amazon SNS (Topic creation, Email subscription, subscription confirmation, and CLI message publication). Construct a complete Amazon VPC networking architecture via CLI (VPC, Subnet, Internet Gateway, Route Table, and route associations). Automate the complete compute lifecycle of Amazon EC2 via CLI (Key Pair creation, Security Group configuration, opening inbound port 22, executing run-instances, allocating/associating an Elastic IP, SSH verification, and terminating instances). 📊 Provisioned Resource Specifications: Resource Name / Identifier Configuration & Detailed Specs Region Notes IAM Group aws-cli Policy: AdministratorAccess Global Centralized privilege management IAM User 1 aws-cli-user Group: aws-cli + CLI Access Key Global Configured for default profile IAM User 2 devops Group: aws-cli + CLI Access Key Global Configured for --profile devops EC2 Management aws-cli-instance t3.micro, Amazon Linux 2023, Key: aws-cli-keypair us-east-1 Bastion workstation connected via MobaXterm Management Subnet subnet-01 CIDR: 172.31.100.0/24, Auto-assign Public IP: Yes us-east-1 Subnet with Internet Gateway routing S3 Bucket aws-cli-trangiabao-2026 Standard Storage, Globally unique bucket name ap-southeast-1 Object storage for testing file text.txt SNS Topic aws-cli ARN: arn:aws:sns:ap-southeast-1:887086382708:aws-cli ap-southeast-1 Notification topic for email alerts VPC (via CLI) vpc-07ebcfa7f5b9c659c CIDR: 10.0.0.0/16 ap-southeast-1 Isolated custom network infrastructure Subnet (via CLI) subnet-03c90d43fb1f53b06 CIDR: 10.0.1.0/24, AZ: ap-southeast-1a ap-southeast-1 Subnet hosting CLI-provisioned EC2 Internet Gateway igw-006783ef67381e1d4 Attached to vpc-07ebcfa7f5b9c659c ap-southeast-1 VPC Internet egress gateway Route Table (CLI) rtb-xxxx Route: 0.0.0.0/0 targeted to Internet Gateway ap-southeast-1 Routes internet traffic for custom subnet Key Pair (CLI) MyKeyPair Type: RSA, file saved as: MyKeyPair.pem (chmod 400) ap-southeast-1 SSH credential for automated EC2 Security Group SSHAccess Inbound: Port 22 (TCP) from 0.0.0.0/0 ap-southeast-1 Firewall rule allowing remote SSH Automated EC2 i-03171455cd0278073 t2.micro, Private IP: 10.0.1.41 ap-southeast-1 Automated EC2 instance launched via CLI Elastic IP 47.131.189.63 Allocation: eipalloc-0f52955fe9fe8ad41 ap-southeast-1 Public IP attached to access instance 📋 Section 1: Prerequisites & Identity Setup Step 1: Create an IAM User Group Action: Log in to the AWS Management Console ➔ Navigate to IAM ➔ In the left navigation pane, select User groups ➔ Click Create group. Purpose: Establish a centralized group for granting administrative privileges to CLI users. Step 2: Configure Group Parameters for aws-cli Input Parameters: User group name: aws-cli Attach permissions policies: Search and select AdministratorAccess. Action: Scroll to the bottom and click Create group. Step 3: Create IAM User aws-cli-user Action: In the left navigation pane, select Users ➔ Click Create user. Input Parameters: User name: aws-cli-user Add user to group: Check the aws-cli group created in Step 2. Action: Click Next ➔ Click Create user. Step 4: Provision CLI Access Key for aws-cli-user Action: Click on user aws-cli-user ➔ Open the Security credentials tab ➔ Scroll down to Access keys ➔ Click Create access key. Options Selected: Use case: Select Command Line Interface (CLI). Confirmation: Check “I understand the above recommendation…”. Action: Click Next ➔ Click Create access key ➔ Download the .csv file containing the Access key ID and Secret access key. Step 5: Create Second IAM User devops for Multi-Profile Action: Repeat the user creation process for a second user named devops. Input Parameters: User name: devops User group: Assign to group aws-cli. Access Key: Generate a separate CLI Access Key pair and save securely. Step 6: Launch EC2 Management Workstation (aws-cli-instance) Action: Open the EC2 console ➔ Click Instances ➔ Click Launch instances. Specific Parameters: Name: aws-cli-instance Application and OS Images (AMI): Select Amazon Linux 2023 kernel-6.1 AMI. Instance type: t3.micro (or t2.micro). Key pair (login): Click Create new key pair ➔ Name it aws-cli-keypair, type RSA, format .pem ➔ Download to local disk. Network settings: Click Edit and configure: VPC: Select your default VPC (vpc-0fc9d5490a843944e). Subnet: Select subnet-01 (CIDR 172.31.100.0/24). Auto-assign public IP: Enable (required to acquire a public IP for SSH). Firewall (Security group): Choose Create security group ➔ Ensure Allow SSH traffic from Anywhere (0.0.0.0/0) is enabled. Action: Click Launch instance. 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Solution at Step 6:
The Subnet field prevented selecting default because default subnets had been deleted during previous lab cleanups.
➔ Solution: Navigated to VPC ➔ Subnets ➔ Clicked Create subnet, created a new subnet named subnet-01 (172.31.100.0/24) in us-east-1a, then selected this subnet in EC2 Network settings with Auto-assign public IP: Enable.
Step 7: Connect via SSH Using MobaXterm Action in MobaXterm: Open MobaXterm ➔ Click Session in the top-left corner ➔ Select SSH. Remote host: Enter the Public IPv4 address of the running instance (e.g. 3.238.185.243 or 32.197.220.215). Specify username: Check and enter ec2-user. Port: 22. Go to Advanced SSH settings ➔ Check Use private key ➔ Select the downloaded file aws-cli-keypair.pem. Click OK ➔ Accept the host key prompt to log in. 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Solution at Step 7:
MobaXterm reported Network error: Connection timed out.
➔ Root Cause: The manually created subnet-01 had no default route to an Internet Gateway.
➔ Solution: In VPC ➔ Internet gateways, created my-igw and attached it to the VPC. In Route tables, edited routes and added Destination: 0.0.0.0/0 targeted to Internet Gateway (igw-xxxx). Pressed R in MobaXterm and connected instantly.
📋 Section 2: Install & Configure AWS CLI v2 Step 8: Install AWS CLI v2 on Linux Commands Executed: Run the following commands on the remote terminal: curl "https://awscli.amazonaws.com/awscli-exe-linux-x86_64.zip" -o "awscliv2.zip" unzip awscliv2.zip sudo ./aws/install aws --version Verification: Terminal prints aws-cli/2.x.x confirming successful installation. Step 9: Configure Default Profile with aws configure Command: aws configure Parameters Entered: AWS Access Key ID [None]: Enter Access Key of aws-cli-user (from Step 4). AWS Secret Access Key [None]: Enter Secret Key of aws-cli-user. Default region name [None]: ap-southeast-1 (Singapore). Default output format [None]: json. Step 10: Configure Named Profile devops Command: aws configure --profile devops Parameters Entered: AWS Access Key ID [None]: Enter Access Key of user devops (from Step 5). AWS Secret Access Key [None]: Enter Secret Key of user devops. Default region name [None]: ap-southeast-1. Default output format [None]: json. Step 11: Inspect Configuration Files and Active Profiles Commands Executed: cat ~/.aws/config cat ~/.aws/credentials aws configure list-profiles Output: Displays separate configurations for default and devops profiles. 📋 Section 3: Verify Resources via CLI Step 12: Query EC2 Instance Details Command Executed: aws ec2 describe-instances --profile devops --region us-east-1 --output table Description: Retrieves all instance metadata in us-east-1 and formats the result as a clear table. 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Solution at Step 12:
Running aws ec2 describe-instances --profile devops initially returned an empty list [].
➔ Root Cause: The devops profile default region is ap-southeast-1 (Singapore), whereas the EC2 management host was launched in us-east-1.
➔ Solution: Explicitly passed --region us-east-1 to query the correct region.
Step 13: List S3 Storage Buckets Command Executed: aws s3 ls --profile devops Output: Lists existing S3 buckets in the AWS account. 📋 Section 4: Administer Amazon S3 via CLI Step 14: Create S3 Bucket and Upload Object Parameters & Commands: Create new bucket: aws s3 mb s3://aws-cli-trangiabao-2026 Create a test file on the EC2 host: echo "Hello AWS S3 from CLI" > text.txt Upload the file to S3: aws s3 cp text.txt s3://aws-cli-trangiabao-2026 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Solution at Step 14:
BucketAlreadyExists Error: Using the tutorial’s sample bucket name aws-cli-2026-18012003 failed because S3 bucket names are globally unique. Solution: Used a custom name aws-cli-trangiabao-2026. NoSuchBucket Error: Copying the placeholder bucket-name caused AWS to look for a non-existent bucket. Solution: Replaced with the exact bucket name s3://aws-cli-trangiabao-2026. Step 15: List Objects and Delete Bucket Commands Executed: List objects: aws s3 ls s3://aws-cli-trangiabao-2026 Delete objects and remove bucket cleanly: aws s3 rb s3://aws-cli-trangiabao-2026 --force 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Solution at Step 15:
Running aws s3 rb s3://... failed with BucketNotEmpty because text.txt was still inside.
➔ Solution: Appended the --force flag to automatically delete all objects prior to bucket deletion.
📋 Section 5: Administer Amazon SNS via CLI Step 16: Create SNS Topic Command Executed: aws sns create-topic --name aws-cli Output: Returns the generated Topic ARN: "TopicArn": "arn:aws:sns:ap-southeast-1:887086382708:aws-cli" Step 17: Subscribe Email Endpoint Command Executed: aws sns subscribe --topic-arn arn:aws:sns:ap-southeast-1:887086382708:aws-cli --protocol email --notification-endpoint trangiabao4461@gmail.com Parameters: --topic-arn: Actual ARN from Step 16. --protocol: email. --notification-endpoint: Target Gmail address. 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Solution at Step 17:
Terminal threw Unknown options: Topic** from copying the bold text **ARN Topic**.
➔ Solution: Replaced **ARN Topic** with the actual Topic ARN string.
Step 18: Pending Confirmation Status Output: Returns "SubscriptionArn": "pending confirmation". Step 19: Confirm Subscription in Gmail Action: Open Gmail, search in:anywhere AWS Notification. Open email from no-reply@sns.amazonaws.com titled AWS Notification - Subscription Confirmation. Click Confirm subscription. Output: Browser displays Subscription confirmed!. 💡 Difficulties Encountered at Step 19: Confirmation email was not in the primary inbox due to a typo in the address and Gmail filtering AWS emails into Spam. Solution: Corrected the typo and searched in Spam folder.
Step 20: Publish Message via CLI Command Executed: aws sns publish --topic-arn arn:aws:sns:ap-southeast-1:887086382708:aws-cli --message "Hello" Output: Terminal outputs a MessageId, and the notification email containing “Hello” is received in the Gmail inbox. 📋 Section 6: Manage IAM via CLI Step 21: List IAM Users Command Executed: aws iam list-users Output: Outputs JSON list of all IAM users with creation dates and ARNs. Step 22: Inspect Policies and Permissions Command Executed: Query policy attachments to verify administrative boundaries. 📋 Section 7: Construct VPC Networking via CLI Step 23: Create VPC Command Executed: aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16 --query Vpc.VpcId --output text Output: Returns VPC ID: vpc-07ebcfa7f5b9c659c. Step 24: Create Subnet Command Executed: aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id vpc-07ebcfa7f5b9c659c --cidr-block 10.0.1.0/24 --query Subnet.SubnetId --output text Output: Returns Subnet ID: subnet-03c90d43fb1f53b06. Step 25: Create Internet Gateway Command Executed: aws ec2 create-internet-gateway --query InternetGateway.InternetGatewayId --output text Output: Returns Internet Gateway ID: igw-006783ef67381e1d4. 💡 Difficulties Encountered at Step 25: IGW did not appear on the AWS Console. Root cause: The CLI created resources in Singapore (ap-southeast-1), while the web console was on N. Virginia (us-east-1). Solution: Switched console region to Singapore.
Step 26: Attach Internet Gateway to VPC Command Executed: aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --vpc-id vpc-07ebcfa7f5b9c659c --internet-gateway-id igw-006783ef67381e1d4 Output: IGW state becomes Attached to vpc-07ebcfa7f5b9c659c. 💡 Note at Step 26: Running this command again produces Resource.AlreadyAssociated. This is an acknowledgment of prior success, not an error.
Step 27: Create Route Table and Add 0.0.0.0/0 Route Commands Executed: Create Route Table: aws ec2 create-route-table --vpc-id vpc-07ebcfa7f5b9c659c --query RouteTable.RouteTableId --output text (Returns Route Table ID rtb-xxxx). Add default route to Internet Gateway: aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id <RTB-ID> --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id igw-006783ef67381e1d4 Step 28: Associate Route Table with Subnet Command Executed: aws ec2 associate-route-table --subnet-id subnet-03c90d43fb1f53b06 --route-table-id <RTB-ID> Output: Successfully binds the subnet to the route table for internet access. 📋 Section 8: Automate EC2 Lifecycle via CLI Step 29: Create Key Pair via CLI Command Executed: aws ec2 create-key-pair --key-name MyKeyPair --query "KeyMaterial" --output text > MyKeyPair.pem Step 30: Set Permissions chmod 400 Command Executed: chmod 400 MyKeyPair.pem Step 31: Create Security Group SSHAccess Command Executed: aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name SSHAccess --description "Security group for SSH access" --vpc-id vpc-07ebcfa7f5b9c659c Output: Returns Security Group ID (e.g. sg-08d6567ccc7edc1f0). Step 32: Authorize Inbound SSH Port 22 Command Executed: aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id <SG-ID> --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0 Step 33: Launch EC2 Instance via run-instances Command Executed: aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-0a37aadea3f79d3c3 --count 1 --instance-type t2.micro --key-name MyKeyPair --security-group-ids <SG-ID> --subnet-id subnet-03c90d43fb1f53b06 Output: Returns Instance ID: i-03171455cd0278073, Private IP: 10.0.1.41. Step 34: Check Instance State Command Executed: aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-id i-03171455cd0278073 --query "Reservations[*].Instances[*].{State:State.Name,Address:PublicIpAddress}" Output: Returns "State": "running", but "Address": null. 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Solution at Step 34:
The query returned "Address": null because subnets created via CLI do not map public IPs by default (MapPublicIpOnLaunch: false).
➔ Solution: Allocated an Elastic IP and associated it directly to the instance without re-creating it (executed in Steps 35 & 36).
Step 35: Allocate Elastic IP Command Executed: aws ec2 allocate-address --domain vpc Output: Public IP: 47.131.189.63, AllocationId: eipalloc-0f52955fe9fe8ad41. Step 36: Associate Elastic IP to Instance i-03171455cd0278073 Command Executed: aws ec2 associate-address --instance-id i-03171455cd0278073 --allocation-id eipalloc-0f52955fe9fe8ad41 💡 Difficulties Encountered at Step 36: Running the SSH command before running associate-address caused the terminal to hang indefinitely. Used Ctrl + C to interrupt, associated the IP first, and then connected.
Step 37: Connect to New EC2 Instance via SSH Command Executed: ssh -i "MyKeyPair.pem" ec2-user@47.131.189.63 Action: Type yes when prompted. Result: Connected successfully! Prompt changes to [ec2-user@ip-10-0-1-41 ~]$. Step 38: Exit and Safely Terminate Instance Commands Executed: Exit guest instance: exit (Returns to management host prompt: [ec2-user@ip-172-31-100-172 ~]$). Terminate instance: aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids i-03171455cd0278073 Result: Instance transitions to shutting-down and terminated. 💡 Difficulties Encountered at Step 38: Running terminate-instances inside the newly provisioned instance (ip-10-0-1-41) returned Unable to locate credentials. Typed exit to return to the management host and executed the command successfully.
🏆 Key Takeaways & Lessons Learned: Accurate Parameter Passing: Learned to extract output values dynamically using --query ... --output text for subsequent CLI commands. Real-world Network Debugging: Diagnosed and rectified multiple AWS network hurdles including missing route table targets, public IP mapping flags, and Elastic IP association workflows. Infrastructure Automation Readiness: Built end-to-end operational confidence to replace manual GUI clicks with structured, reusable command line automation scripts.

title: Amazon Lightsail Container Deployment
content:
The Amazon Lightsail Container Deployment (Run Apps on Lightsail Container) hands-on lab was conducted on Tuesday (06/10/2026) during Week 4. This page provides a thorough step-by-step implementation guide featuring precise parameters, CLI execution commands, troubleshooting solutions, and all 11 verification screenshots. 🔗 Lab Reference Material: Amazon Lightsail Container - Run Apps on Lightsail Container
🎯 Lab Objectives: Familiarize with the Containers feature on Amazon Lightsail — a streamlined solution for running containerized workloads without orchestrator complexity. Install and configure the AWS CLI and the Lightsail Control (lightsailctl) extension plugin to interact with container services from a local workstation. Provision a Container Service on Lightsail utilizing a cost-optimized hardware tier (Nano bundle). Deploy a Public Container Image (Nginx) sourced from Docker Hub onto the Lightsail Container Service. Launch a dedicated virtual machine Build-Instance (Ubuntu) to compile and push a Custom Container Image to the Lightsail private registry via aws lightsail push-container-image. Enable a Public Endpoint and verify live web application delivery over an auto-managed HTTPS SSL/TLS domain. 📊 Provisioned Resource Specifications: Resource Name / Identifier Configuration & Detailed Specs Address / Ports Notes AWS CLI Version 2.37.9 Installed via PowerShell, configured Profile IAM User: Bao (ap-southeast-1) AWS command-line management tool Container Service lightsail-container Nano (512 MB RAM, 0.25 vCPUs x 1 node) Singapore (ap-southeast-1a) Status: Running Public Deployment test1 Image: nginx (Docker Hub Public Registry) Port 80 (HTTP), Health check: / Rapid deployment from public registry Build Instance Build-Instance Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, 512 MB RAM, 20 GB SSD Public IP: 47.129.162.155 Used to build & push Docker images Stored Container :lightsail-container.nginx-container-hello.1 Custom image uploaded from build instance SHA256 digest validation Lightsail private container repository Public Domain lightsail-container...amazonlightsail.com HTTPS auto-issued with AWS SSL certificate Port 443 / 80 Publicly accessible application endpoint 🚀 Step-by-Step Implementation & Screenshot Gallery: Step 1: Install AWS CLI v2 on Windows Workstation Action / Navigation: Open PowerShell with administrative privileges (Run as Administrator) ➔ Execute the automated installation command for AWS CLI v2. Command Executed: irm https://awscli.amazonaws.com/v2/install.ps1 | iex Purpose: Establish a standardized CLI environment to authenticate, manage resources, and push Docker images to Lightsail. Step 2: Verify AWS CLI Installation Version Action / Navigation: Relaunch the terminal window and run the version inspection command. Command Executed: aws --version Output: Displays aws-cli/2.37.9 Python/3.14.0 Windows/10 exe/AMD64, confirming operational readiness. Step 3: Configure AWS Access Credentials (aws configure) Action / Navigation: Run aws configure and input IAM user authentication parameters. Configuration Parameters: AWS Access Key ID: Supply Access Key for IAM User Bao AWS Secret Access Key: Supply matching Secret Access Key Default region name: ap-southeast-1 (Singapore) Default output format: json Command Executed: aws configure Step 4: Verify IAM User Privileges & Resolve AccessDenied Errors Action / Navigation: Test service connectivity using aws s3 ls. Issue Observed: Returns An error occurred (AccessDenied) when calling the ListBuckets operation. Resolution: Navigate to IAM Management Console ➔ Locate User Bao ➔ Select Add permissions ➔ Directly attach policy AmazonLightsailFullAccess and re-verify CLI execution. 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Troubleshooting at Step 4:
When operating Lightsail through the CLI, standard EC2/S3 permissions are insufficient. Commands like aws lightsail push-container-image will immediately fail unless AmazonLightsailFullAccess is granted to allow container service provisioning and private registry image uploads.
Step 5: Provision Container Service on Amazon Lightsail Action / Navigation: Log into the Amazon Lightsail console ➔ Navigate to the Containers tab ➔ Click Create container service. Configuration Parameters: Region: Singapore (ap-southeast-1) Capacity Bundle: Nano (512 MB RAM, 0.25 vCPUs x 1 node) at $7/month for cost optimization Container service name: lightsail-container Result: The service initializes with status Ready and auto-generates a public domain name in the format lightsail-container.<id>.ap-southeast-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com. Step 6: Create First Deployment using Public Nginx Container Image Action / Navigation: In the lightsail-container details view, click Create your first deployment. Configuration Parameters: Container name: test1 Image: nginx (pulled directly from Docker Hub Public Registry) Open ports: Port 80, Protocol HTTP Step 7: Configure Public Endpoint & Health Check Parameters Action / Navigation: Scroll down to the PUBLIC ENDPOINT section on the deployment form. Configuration Parameters: Target container: Select test1 Port: 80 Health check path: / Next Action: Click Save and deploy. Step 8: Validate Active Deployment & Running Service Status Action / Navigation: Monitor the dashboard as Lightsail orchestrates the container lifecycle. Observation: The deployment switches to Active, and overall service status shifts from Deploying to Running. Step 9: Launch Dedicated Build Virtual Machine (Build-Instance) Action / Navigation: Navigate to the Instances tab on Lightsail ➔ Click Create instance to provision a Linux build workstation. Configuration Parameters: Platform: Linux/Unix Blueprint: OS Only ➔ Select Ubuntu 22.04 LTS Instance plan: $3.50/month bundle (512 MB RAM, 1 vCPU, 20 GB SSD) Instance name: Build-Instance Assigned Public IP: 47.129.162.155 Step 10: Build Custom Container Image & Push to Lightsail Registry Action / Navigation: SSH into Build-Instance, install Docker engine, install the lightsailctl plugin, and execute the push command. Commands Executed: # 1. Install lightsailctl extension binary sudo curl "https://s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/lightsailctl/latest/linux-amd64/lightsailctl" -o "/usr/local/bin/lightsailctl" sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/lightsailctl # 2. Build local custom Docker image docker build -t nginx-container-hello:latest . # 3. Push container image directly to Lightsail service repository aws lightsail push-container-image \ --region ap-southeast-1 \ --service-name lightsail-container \ --label nginx-container-hello \ --image nginx-container-hello:latest Result: CLI outputs the stored image reference: :lightsail-container.nginx-container-hello.1 with SHA256 digest. 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Troubleshooting at Step 10:
Missing the lightsailctl binary causes aws lightsail push-container-image to abort immediately because the standard AWS CLI relies on this extension to stream image layers into Lightsail. Ensure execution permissions (chmod +x) are applied and verify location at /usr/local/bin/lightsailctl. Furthermore, the --label flag strictly accepts lowercase letters and hyphens.
Step 11: Update Deployment & Validate Live HTTPS Application Action / Navigation: In the Lightsail Console, update the deployment image source to :lightsail-container.nginx-container-hello.1 ➔ Click Save and deploy ➔ Access the public domain in a browser. Access URL: https://lightsail-container.5vpta1mr2570.ap-southeast-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com Result: Web page loads with the “Welcome to nginx!” landing page, showing a valid SSL/TLS lock icon issued by Amazon Trust Services. 📝 Summary & Key Takeaways: Frictionless Container Deployment: Lightsail Containers provides an effortless abstraction over containerized workloads, removing the overhead of managing Kubernetes control planes (EKS) or complex task definitions (ECS). Automated SSL/TLS Provisioning: Amazon Lightsail automatically provisions free HTTPS endpoints with valid certificates for every service, streamlining production-like testing. Dedicated Build Workstation Pattern: Utilizing a lightweight Lightsail instance (Build-Instance) as a dedicated Docker compiler isolates local development dependencies from cloud deployment pipelines.

title: Event 2
content:
This event report documents the executive fireside chat held directly with Dr. Werner Vogels (Vice President & Chief Technology Officer at Amazon.com) and the AWS Community & Builders in Vietnam on October 02, 2026. It captures foundational architectural lessons on distributed systems at planetary scale, the historical genesis of Amazon DynamoDB, the operational resilience of GameDays, the philosophy of “The Renaissance Developer,” and the evolving role of software engineers in the Generative AI era.
Executive Summary: “The Renaissance Developer & Building for People” – In Conversation with Dr. Werner Vogels (CTO of Amazon) 📌 Event Overview Event Title: Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner Vogels: The Renaissance Developer & Building at Scale. Date & Time: 09:00 - 10:30, October 02, 2026. Location: 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, 02 Hai Trieu Street, Ben Nghe Ward, District 1, Ho Chi Minh City. Keynote Speaker: Dr. Werner Vogels – Vice President & Chief Technology Officer (CTO) at Amazon.com. Moderator / Host: AWS Community Representatives, AWS Heroes & Community Builders Vietnam. Audience: AWS Community Builders, AWS Heroes, cloud architects, industry practitioners, and cloud intern engineers. Participant Role: Attendee / Intern Cloud Builder. 🎯 Key Event Objectives Direct Insights from the Chief Architect of Amazon & AWS: Uncovering firsthand, authentic engineering retrospectives detailing Amazon’s architectural transition from monolithic systems to decoupled, globally distributed infrastructure. Internalizing Amazon’s Product Philosophy: Deep-diving into the Working Backwards framework, rigorous tail-latency management at the 99.9th percentile (P99.9), and chaos engineering drills (GameDays). Defining “The Renaissance Developer”: Identifying the indispensable competencies that keep software engineers relevant, resilient, and empowered alongside rapid advancements in Generative AI. Bridging Global Cloud Leadership with Local Builder Culture: Celebrating the vibrant Vietnamese builder ecosystem (“A nation of builders, and a nation of coffee”), cultural connection through traditional drip coffee, and fostering professional pride among aspiring engineers. 💡 Core Takeaways Extracted from the Fireside Chat 1. The Genesis of Amazon DynamoDB: Lessons from a Catastrophic Holiday Outage The Historical Bottleneck: In the early 2000s, Amazon ran a promotional initiative offering free shipping on purchases exceeding $25 with delivery within two weeks. December 12 was the annual Christmas order cutoff date—the highest traffic shopping day of the entire year. Catastrophic Database Outage: A shared-disk commercial relational database cluster (RDBMS) storing core customer records encountered a severe concurrency bug under peak load, collapsing completely and remaining unavailable for an entire day. Amazon suffered millions of dollars in lost revenue. The Candid Retrospective: When vendor leadership convened with Werner, their initial response was: “You should have tested better!” While humbling, the vendor was right: Amazon was deploying commercial relational software far beyond its designed architectural boundaries. Groundbreaking Access-Pattern Research: Werner tasked Swami Sivasubramanian (then an Amazon intern, currently Vice President of AI at AWS) with auditing Amazon’s actual relational database usage patterns: 70% of access patterns: Were purely simple Key-Value operations (e.g., shopping cart retrieval requiring only a CustomerID; nobody was querying complex relational joins like “list all shopping carts containing a Harry Potter book”). 20% of workloads: Were single-table lookups requiring no relational joins. Only 10% of queries: Truly exercised relational schema capabilities. The Paradigm Shift: Using an expensive, monolithic relational engine for predominantly key-value workloads was an anti-pattern. Amazon committed to engineering its own purpose-built distributed storage engine, publishing the foundational Dynamo paper (2007), which paved the way for the fully managed Amazon DynamoDB service. 2. Operational Excellence & The Reality of Tail Latency (P99.9) The Median Latency Fallacy: Werner highlighted a common engineering blind spot: Measuring website responsiveness via median latency (e.g., 1.5 seconds) is fundamentally misleading. A median of 1.5 seconds means that 50% of your customers are experiencing worse performance! True operational excellence requires optimizing for the 99.9th Percentile (P99.9). Modern cloud architectures must be engineered to compress the entire tail latency distribution, guaranteeing that even the most impacted 0.1% of users experience responsive systems. GameDays and Chaos Engineering: Systems must be architected to withstand losing one or even two data centers (Availability Zones) simultaneously with zero customer disruption. Amazon instituted regular GameDays: Intentionally severing network connectivity or abruptly shutting down an entire data center without prior warning to test real-world failover automation. The Overlooked Challenge of Recovery & Reconciliation: While automated failover to remaining healthy data centers was quickly mastered, the team initially overlooked how to safely reconcile and bring the recovered data center back online with consistent state. Lesson: Architecting for failure requires not just surviving outages, but engineering complete, automated data reconciliation pipelines when disrupted infrastructure recovers. 3. Transforming Enterprise Cloud Economics Disrupting Long-Term Vendor Lock-in: Werner recalled that in his early years as CTO, vendor negotiations were fraught with predatory 5-to-10-year contracts requiring millions of dollars in upfront capital expenditure (CapEx) before technology was even deployed. The “Zero-Deposit Restaurant” Analogy: Werner analogized traditional IT procurement: Nobody walks into a restaurant in Vietnam and places 500,000 VND on the table before even knowing what food is served. AWS revolutionized IT by introducing true utility pricing: Pay-as-you-go—paying only for actual resource consumption with zero contractual obligations. Customers hold complete freedom to migrate away at any time, forcing cloud providers to continuously deliver operational value daily. S3’s Original Mission: When Amazon S3 launched in 2006, its tagline was simply “Storage for the Internet”—democratizing limitless scale for young web startups rather than catering solely to legacy corporate data centers. 4. The Profile of “The Renaissance Developer” Drawing from his landmark AWS re:Invent keynote, Werner elaborated on five vital qualities defining resilient engineering professionals:
Curiosity & Lifelong Learning: Tracing his own evolution from Pascal, COBOL, and Assembly to C, C++, Java, Python, and Rust, Werner stated that engineers must remain professional students throughout their careers. Quoting Rear Admiral Grace Hopper: “The most dangerous phrase in the language is, ‘We’ve always done it this way.’” Avoid locking your engineering identity into being just a “Java shop” or “Python shop.” System Thinking: Cultivate the ability to see the holistic architectural picture, understanding how discrete distributed services interact rather than narrowing focus to a single microservice or function. Communication – The Most Underrated Skill: Dispel the cinema stereotype of the isolated programmer coding in a dark basement. Engineers must excel at bridging customer problems and business objectives. When stakeholders demand “We need to use AI for this,” skilled engineers drill down to uncover the underlying challenge, evaluating whether complex models are truly required or if straightforward tools (like Amazon Rekognition) suffice. Uncompromising Ownership: Core tenet: “You own what you build.” Even when utilizing AI tools (Copilot, Claude, Cursor) to generate boilerplate code, any resulting bugs, performance regressions, or security vulnerabilities remain 100% your responsibility. Engineers cannot abdicate accountability to an AI tool. Polymath / T-Shaped Breadth: Cultivate deep specialization in a primary domain (e.g., distributed databases) while maintaining sufficient breadth across UI, networking, and business logic to collaborate seamlessly across cross-functional teams. 5. Artificial Intelligence: An Amplifier for Human Ingenuity AI in Perspective: Artificial Intelligence is not a novel phenomenon of the last two years; the discipline originated in 1956 with John McCarthy and Marvin Minsky. As McCarthy famously remarked: “As soon as it works, we don’t call it AI anymore”—it becomes standard search, computer vision, or forecasting algorithms. AI as a Next-Generation Compiler: Traditional compilers take precise, structured programming language code and emit machine code that humans do not need to inspect. Generative AI operates inversely: It receives imprecise natural language prompts and generates structured source code. Because natural language is inherently ambiguous, AI cannot say “I don’t know” and will hallucinate. Therefore, human code reviews and rigorous automated verification are non-negotiable. Amazon’s “Working Backwards” Framework: Long before writing implementation code, teams author a mock Press Release and Customer FAQs (PR/FAQ). Generative AI accelerates early-stage prototyping, compressing weeks of proof-of-concept development into hours. Human-Centric Technology Philosophy: “We build technology for people, not for technology’s sake.”
Technology is ultimately a tool. Enduring engineering value stems from uniquely human traits: Sound Judgment, Empathy, Intuitive Insight, and Professional Pride. 🎁 Cultural Highlight: Connecting with the Vietnam Builder Community Representatives from the AWS Vietnam Community presented Dr. Werner Vogels with a traditional Vietnamese Phin Coffee Filter set paired with premium local coffee beans. Werner enthusiastically shared his appreciation for “Cà phê sữa đá” (Vietnamese iced milk coffee) and praised the energy, humility, and technical ambition of Vietnam’s growing builder community. Closing message: Take pride in community contributions and empower peers so that the entire tech ecosystem scales collectively. 🚀 Direct Application to Cloud Internship & Engineering Practice Incorporating P99.9 Tail Latency Benchmarks: Evaluate deployed architectures beyond simple functional checks by simulating heavy load, tracking percentile metrics via CloudWatch, and calibrating Auto Scaling policies. Practicing Multi-AZ Resilience & Disaster Recovery: Rigorously configure Multi-AZ failover for Amazon RDS and Amazon ElastiCache, while designing explicit data reconciliation procedures for post-incident recovery. Rigorous Accountability with AI-Generated Code: Leverage generative developer tools to amplify productivity while rigorously auditing every generated line of infrastructure-as-code and application logic. Honing Technical Communication: Craft architectural documentation, worklogs, and presentation narratives that are articulate and actionable for both technical and business stakeholders. 📸 Event Photo Highlights & Attendance Proof Below are on-site photographs captured during the Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner Vogels on the 26th Floor of the Bitexco Financial Tower:
1. Dr. Werner Vogels on the Fireside Chat Stage Figure 1: Dr. Werner Vogels (VP & CTO of Amazon.com) in conversation with Nguyen Gia Hung (Solutions Architect Manager) and My Nguyen (Sr Prototyping Architect, AWS Vietnam) at the 26th Floor, Bitexco.
2. Community Group Photo with Dr. Werner Vogels Figure 2: Memorable group photo bringing together AWS Heroes, AWS Community Builders, and First Cloud Journey intern engineers alongside Dr. Werner Vogels.
3. Intern Engineering Cohort at the Event Figure 3: First Cloud Journey intern team checking in at the AWS office (26th floor Bitexco) in front of the Amazon Leadership Principle wall “Invent and Simplify”.
Retrospective: Interacting with Dr. Werner Vogels provided invaluable architectural wisdom and deep inspiration, reinforcing the mindset of continuous learning, rigorous engineering ownership, and human-centric cloud innovation.

title: Week 2
content:
Week 2 Objectives: Master workload optimization principles according to the AWS Well-Architected Framework under the Optimizing the System on AWS curriculum. Explore event-driven serverless operational automation (AWS Lambda), centralized observability, and Infrastructure as Code foundations. Implement cryptographic data protection (AWS KMS), web application perimeter defense (AWS WAF), and continuous threat detection (Amazon GuardDuty). Deploy serverless microservices container packaging (Amazon ECS Fargate) alongside automated Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment pipelines (CI/CD). Formulate long-term cost governance strategies (Savings Plans) and serverless expense telemetry analytics via AWS Glue & Amazon Athena. Dedicate Friday to synthesizing weekly technical knowledge, finalizing comprehensive Worklog documentation, and advancing the internship Capstone Project Proposal. Tasks to be Carried Out This Week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material Monday Operational Excellence & Serverless Automation: - Automating administrative tasks with AWS Lambda (000022). - Advanced observability with CloudWatch & Grafana (000029). - Infrastructure as Code concepts with AWS CloudFormation (000037). 09/21/2026 09/21/2026 Cloud Journey - Operations Tuesday Security & Cryptographic Data Protection: - Centralized encryption key management with AWS KMS (000033). - Web layer perimeter defense using AWS WAF (000026). - Intelligent threat detection with Amazon GuardDuty (000098). 09/22/2026 09/22/2026 Cloud Journey - Security Wednesday Reliability & Serverless Containers: - Microservices containerization via Docker & Amazon ECS Fargate (000016). - Automated software delivery pipelines via AWS CodePipeline (000017). 09/23/2026 09/23/2026 Cloud Journey - Reliability Thursday Cost Optimization & Telemetry Analytics: - Long-term financial commitments via Savings Plans & Reserved Instances (000042). - Serverless cost analytics with AWS Glue & Athena (000040). 09/24/2026 09/24/2026 Cloud Journey - Cost Friday Week 2 Review, Worklog Completion & Project Work: - Knowledge Review: Consolidate the 4 Well-Architected pillars mastered (Operations, Security, Reliability, Cost). - Worklog Completion: Finalize bilingual Week 2 documentation and execute clean resource teardowns. - Project Work: Refine architectural schematics and compute monthly budget models for the Capstone Proposal. 09/25/2026 09/25/2026 FCAJ Roadmap Daily In-Depth Learning Outcomes & Key Takeaways: 📌 Monday (09/21/2026) - Operational Excellence & Serverless Automation What did we learn today? Event-Driven Serverless Compute with AWS Lambda: Mastered serverless compute abstraction: Eliminating OS patching and capacity management, executing code only in response to discrete triggers. Developed an automated maintenance function ec2-nightly-stop in Python using Boto3 to discover development instances matching Environment = Development and issue termination signals at 20:00 daily. Automated Event Scheduling via EventBridge & CloudWatch: Established an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler cron expression cron(0 20 ? * MON-FRI *) invoking the Lambda handler automatically. Streamed execution telemetry into CloudWatch Logs Group /aws/lambda/ec2-nightly-stop, measuring cold-start durations of 1.2 seconds and memory allocations under 64MB. Figure 1.2.1: Automated serverless EC2 operational management triggered by EventBridge and AWS Lambda.
Encountered Challenges & Solutions: AccessDeniedException on Function Execution: The Lambda handler failed with unauthorized API call errors when invoking EC2 APIs. Root cause: Default basic execution roles only permit writing CloudWatch Logs. Solution: Created an IAM customer-managed policy authorizing ec2:DescribeInstances and ec2:StopInstances attached to the function execution role. 📌 Tuesday (09/22/2026) - Security Hardening & Cryptographic Key Management What did we learn today? Envelope Encryption & Lifecycle Governance with AWS KMS: Differentiated between AWS Managed Keys and Customer Managed Keys (CMK). Created symmetric CMK fcaj-data-encryption-key, defining granular Key Policies controlling which IAM principals can invoke kms:Encrypt and kms:Decrypt. Enabled Automatic Annual Key Rotation without changing key ARNs. Applied CMK encryption across Amazon EBS storage volumes and Amazon S3 objects (SSE-KMS) with full audit logging in CloudTrail. Web Application Defense via AWS WAF: Created and deployed a regional Web ACL protecting Application Load Balancers. Configured pre-packaged AWS Managed Rules: Core rule set (CRS) for OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities, Amazon IP reputation list blocking malicious scanners, and a Rate-based rule capping traffic at 100 requests per 5 minutes per IP. Intelligent Threat Detection with Amazon GuardDuty: Activated GuardDuty to passively analyze VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, and CloudTrail management events using machine learning to detect port scans and compromised credentials. Figure 1.2.2: S3 data-at-rest encryption control model governed by AWS KMS and audited via CloudTrail.
Figure 1.2.3: Perimeter defense shield protecting application entry points against web threats using AWS WAF.
Encountered Challenges & Solutions: False-Positive Block on Legitimate API Payloads: Valid client requests were blocked with HTTP 403 by the GenericRFI_BODY rule. Solution: Inspected CloudWatch WAF metrics to identify the specific rule ID, toggled the rule to Count mode to log telemetry without dropping packets, and configured path-specific rule exclusions. 📌 Wednesday (09/23/2026) - Resilience & Serverless Microservices Containers What did we learn today? Serverless Container Orchestration with Amazon ECS Fargate: Packaged microservice application code into Docker images and published versioned artifacts to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR). Authored ECS Task Definitions specifying container compute footprints (0.25 vCPU, 512MB RAM), eliminating underlying host OS administration. Launched an ECS Service running on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer with dynamic health checking and self-healing task replacement. Continuous Delivery Automation via AWS CodePipeline: Engineered an automated CI/CD pipeline: Pulling source updates from GitHub ➔ Triggering AWS CodeBuild to compile Docker images and execute unit tests ➔ Executing rolling deployments to ECS Fargate tasks with zero downtime. Figure 1.2.4: Multi-container service orchestration architecture on Amazon ECS elastically scaled via AWS Fargate.
Figure 1.2.5: Successful automated build and deployment report in AWS CodeBuild.
Encountered Challenges & Solutions: Docker Hub Pull Rate Limiting in CodeBuild: Builds failed during base image acquisition. Solution: Updated Dockerfiles to pull official base images from the Amazon ECR Public Gallery (public.ecr.aws/docker/library/), bypassing third-party rate limits and improving download speeds over AWS internal networks. 📌 Thursday (09/24/2026) - Cost Optimization & Telemetry Analytics What did we learn today? Strategic Cloud Financial Management: Analyzed cost structures across On-Demand, Spot instances (up to 90% discount for fault-tolerant workloads), and 1- to 3-year commitments (Savings Plans & Reserved Instances). For steady-state 24/7 database and backend tiers, Compute Savings Plans yield 45% to 66% sustained cost reductions compared to standard On-Demand pricing. Serverless Telemetry Analytics with AWS Glue & Athena: Configured AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) delivering granular hourly billing manifests into an S3 bucket. Deployed an AWS Glue Crawler to discover report schemas and generate partition metadata in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Executed serverless SQL queries in Amazon Athena to identify spending spikes per service, peak regional usage hours, and unattached idle EBS volumes. Figure 1.2.6: Cloud cost data extraction, cataloging, and analytical query workflow utilizing AWS Glue and Amazon Athena.
Encountered Challenges & Solutions: Athena Syntax Errors Reading Compressed CUR Manifests: Direct queries threw syntax errors on gzipped micro-batch files. Solution: Deployed the automated CloudFormation integration template provided by AWS CUR, configuring standardized month-based partition indexing for Athena. 📌 Friday (09/25/2026) - Week 2 Review, Worklog Finalization & Proposal Formulation What did we learn today? AWS Well-Architected Pillar Synthesis: Operational Excellence: Event-driven automation with Lambda and observability via CloudWatch. Security: Envelope encryption via KMS and perimeter defense via WAF. Reliability: Microservices containerization via ECS Fargate and automated CI/CD deployments. Cost Optimization: Strategic commitment models and serverless billing audits with Athena. Resource Hygiene: Decommissioned test ECS services, halted crawler jobs, and detached staging Web ACLs to preserve financial guardrails. Capstone Proposal Development: Finalized full system architecture blueprints and drafted detailed monthly operational cost projections utilizing the official AWS Pricing Calculator.

title: Creating an S3 Interface Endpoint (AWS PrivateLink)
content:
Step-by-Step Procedure: Open the Amazon VPC Management Console in region us-east-1 (N. Virginia).
In the left navigation pane, select Endpoints and click Create endpoint.
Configure Endpoint Identity:
Name tag: Enter s3-interface-endpoint Service category: Select AWS services Service Selection: In the Services search filter, type s3 and hit Enter. Select service: com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3 Verify the Type column: Ensure the selected row indicates Interface. Network Association: VPC: Select VPC Cloud from the dropdown menu. [!WARNING] Verify you select VPC Cloud. Do not attach this interface endpoint to VPC On-prem.
Expand Additional settings: Ensure Enable DNS name is UNCHECKED (we will simulate custom corporate DNS routing in step 5.4.4). Subnet Placement (Multi-AZ): Select 2 private subnets across two distinct Availability Zones: us-east-1a and us-east-1b for fault tolerance. Security Group Association: Select Security Group: SGforS3Endpoint (configured to permit inbound HTTPS port 443 from internal network CIDRs). Finalize Provisioning: Retain default policy: Full access. Click Create endpoint. The console confirms endpoint creation. Wait approximately 1-2 minutes until status becomes Available.

title: Proposal
content:
⚠️ Note: The information below is for reference purposes only. Please do not copy verbatim for your report, including this warning.
In this section, you need to summarize the contents of the workshop that you plan to conduct.
IoT Weather Platform for Lab Research A Unified AWS Serverless Solution for Real-Time Weather Monitoring 1. Executive Summary The IoT Weather Platform is designed for the ITea Lab team in Ho Chi Minh City to enhance weather data collection and analysis. It supports up to 5 weather stations, with potential scalability to 10-15, utilizing Raspberry Pi edge devices with ESP32 sensors to transmit data via MQTT. The platform leverages AWS Serverless services to deliver real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and cost efficiency, with access restricted to 5 lab members via Amazon Cognito.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? Current weather stations require manual data collection, becoming unmanageable with multiple units. There is no centralized system for real-time data or analytics, and third-party platforms are costly and overly complex.
The Solution The platform uses AWS IoT Core to ingest MQTT data, AWS Lambda and API Gateway for processing, Amazon S3 for storage (including a data lake), and AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to extract, transform, and load data from the S3 data lake to another S3 bucket for analysis. AWS Amplify with Next.js provides the web interface, and Amazon Cognito ensures secure access. Similar to Thingsboard and CoreIoT, users can register new devices and manage connections, though this platform operates on a smaller scale and is designed for private use. Key features include real-time dashboards, trend analysis, and low operational costs.
Benefits and Return on Investment The solution establishes a foundational resource for lab members to develop a larger IoT platform, serving as a study resource, and provides a data foundation for AI enthusiasts for model training or analysis. It reduces manual reporting for each station via a centralized platform, simplifying management and maintenance, and improves data reliability. Monthly costs are $0.66 USD per the AWS Pricing Calculator, with a 12-month total of $7.92 USD. All IoT equipment costs are covered by the existing weather station setup, eliminating additional development expenses. The break-even period of 6-12 months is achieved through significant time savings from reduced manual work.
3. Solution Architecture The platform employs a serverless AWS architecture to manage data from 5 Raspberry Pi-based stations, scalable to 15. Data is ingested via AWS IoT Core, stored in an S3 data lake, and processed by AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to transform and load it into another S3 bucket for analysis. Lambda and API Gateway handle additional processing, while Amplify with Next.js hosts the dashboard, secured by Cognito. The architecture is detailed below:
AWS Services Used AWS IoT Core: Ingests MQTT data from 5 stations, scalable to 15. AWS Lambda: Processes data and triggers Glue jobs (two functions). Amazon API Gateway: Facilitates web app communication. Amazon S3: Stores raw data in a data lake and processed outputs (two buckets). AWS Glue: Crawlers catalog data, and ETL jobs transform and load it. AWS Amplify: Hosts the Next.js web interface. Amazon Cognito: Secures access for lab users. Component Design Edge Devices: Raspberry Pi collects and filters sensor data, sending it to IoT Core. Data Ingestion: AWS IoT Core receives MQTT messages from the edge devices. Data Storage: Raw data is stored in an S3 data lake; processed data is stored in another S3 bucket. Data Processing: AWS Glue Crawlers catalog the data, and ETL jobs transform it for analysis. Web Interface: AWS Amplify hosts a Next.js app for real-time dashboards and analytics. User Management: Amazon Cognito manages user access, allowing up to 5 active accounts. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases This project has two parts—setting up weather edge stations and building the weather platform—each following 4 phases:
Build Theory and Draw Architecture: Research Raspberry Pi setup with ESP32 sensors and design the AWS serverless architecture (1 month pre-internship) Calculate Price and Check Practicality: Use AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate costs and adjust if needed (Month 1). Fix Architecture for Cost or Solution Fit: Tweak the design (e.g., optimize Lambda with Next.js) to stay cost-effective and usable (Month 2). Develop, Test, and Deploy: Code the Raspberry Pi setup, AWS services with CDK/SDK, and Next.js app, then test and release to production (Months 2-3). Technical Requirements
Weather Edge Station: Sensors (temperature, humidity, rainfall, wind speed), a microcontroller (ESP32), and a Raspberry Pi as the edge device. Raspberry Pi runs Raspbian, handles Docker for filtering, and sends 1 MB/day per station via MQTT over Wi-Fi. Weather Platform: Practical knowledge of AWS Amplify (hosting Next.js), Lambda (minimal use due to Next.js), AWS Glue (ETL), S3 (two buckets), IoT Core (gateway and rules), and Cognito (5 users). Use AWS CDK/SDK to code interactions (e.g., IoT Core rules to S3). Next.js reduces Lambda workload for the fullstack web app. 5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline
Pre-Internship (Month 0): 1 month for planning and old station review. Internship (Months 1-3): 3 months. Month 1: Study AWS and upgrade hardware. Month 2: Design and adjust architecture. Month 3: Implement, test, and launch. Post-Launch: Up to 1 year for research. 6. Budget Estimation You can find the detailed budget estimation directly on the AWS Pricing Calculator.
Infrastructure Costs AWS Services: AWS Lambda: $0.00/month (1,000 requests, 512 MB storage). S3 Standard: $0.15/month (6 GB, 2,100 requests, 1 GB scanned). Data Transfer: $0.02/month (1 GB inbound, 1 GB outbound). AWS Amplify: $0.35/month (256 MB, 500 ms requests). Amazon API Gateway: $0.01/month (2,000 requests). AWS Glue ETL Jobs: $0.02/month (2 DPUs). AWS Glue Crawlers: $0.07/month (1 crawler). MQTT (IoT Core): $0.08/month (5 devices, 45,000 messages). Total: $0.7/month, $8.40/12 months
Hardware: $265 one-time (Raspberry Pi 5 and sensors). 7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Network Outages: Medium impact, medium probability. Sensor Failures: High impact, low probability. Cost Overruns: Medium impact, low probability. Mitigation Strategies Network: Local storage on Raspberry Pi with Docker. Sensors: Regular checks and spares. Cost: AWS budget alerts and optimization. Contingency Plans Revert to manual methods if AWS fails. Use CloudFormation for cost-related rollbacks. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements: Real-time data and analytics replace manual processes.
Scalable to 10-15 stations.
Long-term Value 1-year data foundation for AI research.
Reusable for future projects.

content:
Harvest Report: “First Cloud AI Journey” Meetup (October 24, 2026) 📌 Event Overview Event Name: First Cloud AI Journey Meetup: Trends & Real-world Practices in Cloud & AI Agent Deployment Date & Time: 09:00 – 12:00, Saturday Morning, October 24, 2026 Location: AWS Vietnam Office, 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, 02 Hai Trieu Street, Ben Nghe Ward, District 1, Ho Chi Minh City Organizers: First Cloud Journey (FCJ) in collaboration with AWS Community Builders and AWS Student Builder Groups Role: Attendee & First Cloud Journey Intern Audience: Over 100 technology engineers, including Tech Leads, Cloud Solutions Architects, DevOps/Security Engineers from enterprises, AWS Community Builders, alongside passionate students and interns eager to master Cloud Computing and Generative AI Agents. 🎯 Objectives & Expectations Explore Production-grade AI Agent Architectures: Gain deep insights into how industry practitioners combine core AWS cloud infrastructure with modern Generative AI to deploy autonomous agents in production environments. Learn Enterprise-level Technical Solutions: Grasp real-world challenges and concrete technical remedies: optimizing latency for Vietnamese Voice AI, centralized multi-account networking with AWS RAM, automated shift-left security testing with AI Pentesting agents, and context window/memory management. Expand Professional Community Networking: Directly connect and engage with Tech Leads, AWS Community Builders, and senior enterprise engineers to glean career advice and cultivate a mature engineering mindset. 🎤 In-Depth Technical Sessions Breakdown The meetup delivered condensed, highly actionable technical insights through five curated sessions:
1. Session 1: Hear, Think, Speak - Building a Vietnamese Voice-AI Contact Center on AWS Mr. Kiet Tran (Founder & AI Engineer at Revve AI) detailing the architectural nuances between Cascade, Speech-to-Speech (S2S), and Full-duplex S2S voice systems.
Speaker: Mr. Kiet Tran – Founder & AI Engineer at Revve AI. Core Technical Insights: Three Architectural Paradigms for Voice Agents: Cascade Pipeline: Serial chaining of ASR (Speech-to-Text) ➔ LLM (Text-to-Text) ➔ TTS (Text-to-Speech). Key advantage: an explicit text checkpoint in the middle enabling strict guardrail enforcement and auditability. Speech-to-Speech (S2S): A unified speech model (e.g., Amazon Nova 2 Sonic) ingesting raw audio and outputting direct speech. Operates in half-duplex mode: user barge-in immediately interrupts and halts bot audio playback. Full-duplex S2S: Continuous bidirectional audio streaming (e.g., OpenAI Realtime, Gemini Live), empowering the bot to respond naturally with backchannel interjections (“yes”, “uh-huh”) and seamless vocal overlap just like human conversation. Four Practical Lessons Paid in Production: Vietnamese Tone & Turn Detection Accuracy (79% vs 94%): Vietnamese acoustic intonation and tone diacritics cause high false cut-off rates under English-centric algorithms ➔ Mandatory requirement to benchmark directly on native Vietnamese audio datasets. Raw Number Pronunciation Quirks (“500K” read as abbreviation instead of “five hundred thousand”): Untreated text fed to TTS engines leads to mispronunciations ➔ Requires a dedicated Text Normalization layer prior to speech synthesis. Sentence-level Guardrails (Guard per Sentence): Streaming output without fine-grained checkpoints risks playing inappropriate opening words to callers (5 out of 6 leak cases). Enforcing an intermediate Small Judge Model to evaluate each sentence before TTS reduced violations to 0 out of 6. Latency Budget Management: Strict constraint to cap total round-trip latency under ~1.8s for smooth conversational flow, mandating a median LLM latency budget between 0.24s and 1.15s (e.g., self-hosted Gemma models). Live Demo: Live automated phone call interview screening a candidate for a Cloud Engineer position in natural Vietnamese, demonstrating fluid turn-taking, prompt understanding, and context-aware responses. 2. Session 2: AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) - Create Once, Share Everywhere Mr. Long Huynh (Solutions Engineer at Styl Solution) addressing multi-account infrastructure fragmentation and demonstrating how AWS RAM enables centralized, cost-effective resource sharing.
Speaker: Mr. Long Huynh – Solutions Engineer at Styl Solution. Core Technical Insights: The Multi-Account Challenge: In enterprise environments spanning multiple AWS accounts (for different departments, business units, or SDLC stages like Dev, Staging, and Production), duplicating shared network infrastructure (Transit Gateways, VPC Subnets, Route 53 Resolver Rules, License Manager) incurs 3x cost inflation, configuration drift, and decentralized governance. The AWS RAM Paradigm: Implements the core principle: “Create once, share securely across the entire organization (AWS Organizations)”. Infrastructure is provisioned once within an authoritative Owner Account and shared seamlessly via Resource Shares to Member Accounts. Consumer Accounts consume these shared assets natively within their own AWS Console interfaces without administrative overhead. Dual-layer Governance (IAM Policies combined with SCPs): Combines granular IAM Resource-based Policies with organization-wide Service Control Policies (SCPs) to establish immutable permission guardrails, preventing member accounts from altering or bypassing shared network topologies. 3. Session 3: AWS Pentest with AWS Continuum / Security Agent Mr. Nguyen Tuan Thinh (Security Engineer at Styl Solution) engaging with audience inquiries regarding autonomous security agents and automated CI/CD pentesting on SIT/UAT.
Speaker: Mr. Nguyen Tuan Thinh – Security Engineer at Styl Solution. Core Technical Insights: The Shift-Left Security Philosophy: Embedding security verification into the earliest phases of the software development lifecycle (SDLC) rather than treating it as an afterthought before release. Automated Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) Auditing: Integrating automated security bots into GitHub and GitLab Pull Request (PR) pipelines. Performing Static Code Analysis on Terraform scripts to detect vulnerabilities such as unrestricted 0.0.0.0/0 ingress rules, unencrypted EBS volumes/S3 buckets, or overprivileged wildcard IAM policies (*) before code is merged. Frontier Security Agent: Powered by Amazon Bedrock foundation models with autonomous reasoning capabilities to plan and execute comprehensive security evaluations without human intervention. Acts as an active simulated adversary (Attacker) performing penetration testing against SIT and UAT staging environments to uncover business logic flaws and configuration oversights before production deployment. 4. Session 4: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore - Production Architecture & Dual Memory System Mr. Xuan An (Leader of AWS Student Builder Group HCMUTE) explaining single-session ephemeral MicroVMs on EC2 Spot instances for cost-optimized agent runtimes.
Speaker: Mr. Xuan An – Leader of AWS Student Builder Group HCMUTE. Core Technical Insights: Agent Ecosystem Architecture: A modular framework harmonizing Application Layer ➔ Agent Runtime (framework, instructions, local tools, context) ➔ Foundation Models. Cost-effective Agent Runtime on EC2 Spot Instances: Instead of maintaining expensive, long-running servers, the runtime orchestrates lightweight MicroVMs dynamically provisioned on Amazon EC2 Spot Instances. Ephemeral Context Principle: “Micro lives to serve a single session only” – Each MicroVM encapsulates session data (Disk and Memory) exclusively for the duration of one user dialogue. Upon session completion, the instance is promptly recycled, slashing operational compute expenses by 70% to 90%. Dual-tier Memory System: Short-term Memory: Synchronous in-session state retention to maintain immediate conversational context. Long-term Memory: Asynchronous post-session extraction of user preferences, core facts, and critical historical decisions into Vector Databases (OpenSearch / Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases) to ensure persistent personalization across subsequent interactions. 5. Session 5: Kiro Crew - All-In-One AI Companion for Engineers Mr. Danh Hoang Hieu Nghi (AWS Community Builder) and Mr. Kieu Nguyen Dang Khoa (Tech Lead ACB) demonstrating live developer storage inspection and token breakdown.
Speakers: Mr. Kieu Nguyen Dang Khoa (Technical Lead – Digital Transformation at ACB Bank) & Mr. Danh Hoang Hieu Nghi (AWS Community Builder). Core Technical Insights & Live Demonstrations: 24/7 Engineer Companion: Platform architecture designed to continuously assist software engineers with code reviews, architectural compliance checks, and infrastructure health monitoring. Automated Visual UI Artifacts Generation: Demonstrating an end-to-end workflow where the agent autonomously crawls real-world tech job market listings, synthesizes key data points, and renders interactive UI chart artifacts directly inside the chat interface. Context Window Management Strategies: Auto Compact Mechanism: Automatically triggered when conversation context reaches 70% – 90% of model token limits, intelligently summarizing earlier dialogue turns to liberate token capacity without dropping conversational coherence. Context Breakdown Inspector: Enables engineers to dissect token consumption across System Prompts, Tool/Function Schemas, Memory, and User Messages, facilitating cost and performance tuning. Developer Storage Management & Security Guardrails: Selective memory cleanup algorithms targeting stale or unneeded storage keys to avoid database bloat. Robust Guardrails: Enforcing strict execution policies that prohibit destructive commands (such as terminating core instances or dropping database schemas) and sanitize model responses to prevent secret/credential leakage (AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, API tokens). 💡 Key Takeaways & Lessons Learned FinOps & Latency Budget Trade-offs: In Voice AI and real-time agent workflows, every millisecond counts. Model selection (Cascade vs S2S, Cloud APIs vs Self-hosted Open Source) must be strictly governed by latency thresholds and cost-efficiency rather than chasing parameter size blindly. Centralized Multi-Account Governance with AWS RAM: Enterprise architectures demand centralized resource ownership combined with seamless distributed consumption. Combining AWS RAM with SCPs provides a battle-tested blueprint for scalable multi-account organizations. Empowering Security via Autonomous Shift-Left Agents: Security testing is evolving from manual periodic audits into automated, agentic CI/CD verifications, identifying infrastructure vulnerabilities before code reaches production environments. Mastering Agent Context and Memory Hygiene: Implementing dynamic context compaction (Auto Compact) alongside dual-tier memory structures (Short-term vs Long-term) is crucial for delivering highly capable, cost-efficient, and reliable AI systems. 🚀 Practical Application to FCJ Internship & Cloud Projects Implement Safety Guardrails in Automated Scripts: Always incorporate pre-flight validation checks and safety boundaries into automated infrastructure scripts to prevent unintended modifications or deletions. Architect Scalable and Secure Cloud Networking: Apply learnings regarding VPC Subnet grouping, Route Table isolation, and AWS RAM multi-account sharing to future multi-tier architecture labs in Weeks 6 through 12. Embrace the Renaissance Developer Mindset: Actively participate in AWS Community meetups to broaden technical perspectives, bridge the gap between cloud infrastructure and emerging AI agent paradigms, and foster continuous learning. 📸 Event Photo Gallery & Proof of Attendance 1.
