2. Group Photos & Event Atmosphere Figure 2: Memorable group photo capturing over 100 participants, including speakers, organizers, AWS Community Builders, and enthusiastic interns.
Figure 3: All attendees waving to commemorate an inspiring, high-energy Saturday morning meetup.
Conclusion: The “First Cloud AI Journey” Meetup was an extraordinarily enriching experience. Bridging foundational cloud infrastructure with the forefront of generative AI agent development, the event instilled valuable practical knowledge and immense inspiration for aspiring cloud engineers. It reinforced the determination to remain proactive, continuously learn, and confidently progress on the journey to mastering the cloud.

title: AWS Tags and Resource Groups Management
content:
The AWS Tags and Resource Groups Management hands-on lab was conducted on Wednesday (21/10/2026) as part of Week 6. This document provides an exhaustive step-by-step implementation guide for metadata categorization using AWS Tags, command-line automation via the AWS CLI, and centralized infrastructure governance using AWS Resource Groups.
🎯 Lab Objectives: Understand the strategic importance of AWS Tags in cloud governance, operational automation, cost allocation tracking, and Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC). Practice manual tag assignment and tag lifecycle management through the Amazon EC2 Management Console across multiple instances. Master command-line tag administration via the AWS CLI: generate dedicated IAM credentials, configure local profiles, execute atomic create-tags operations, and construct complex query expressions using describe-instances --filters. Architect and provision AWS Resource Groups: create a tag-based group named EnvTest to automatically aggregate compute instances sharing common environmental metadata. Analyze real-world troubleshooting scenarios: tag key case-sensitivity, tag volume limits, CLI parameter escaping in PowerShell, and regional boundaries of resource groups. 📊 Provisioned Resource Specifications: Component / Resource Identifier (Name / ID) Configuration & Assigned Tags Region Operational Purpose EC2 Instance 1 ec2-instance-1 (i-02b440e03f77f9942) Environment: Test
Service: YourService
Owner: YourName
OS: Amazon Linux us-east-1a Test Instance 1, managed via Web Console EC2 Instance 2 ec2-instance-2 (i-0abb0b1178954e0a4) Project: AWS
Env: Test us-east-1a Test Instance 2, tagged programmatically via AWS CLI EC2 Instance 3 ec2-instance-3 (i-00ecbe56e33f40770) Environment: Test
Name: ec2-instance-3 us-east-1a Launched and labeled via AWS CLI IAM Access Key AKIA_DEMO_SAMPLE_KEY_ID Programmatic credentials for user trangiabao Global Secure authentication for AWS CLI workstation AWS Resource Group EnvTest Group Type: Tag based
Query: AWS::EC2::Instance with tag Environment: Test us-east-1 Centralized group view for test environment instances 🚀 Step-by-Step Implementation & Verification: Section 1: Tag Administration via AWS Management Console Step 1: Launch EC2 Instances and Verify Initial State Action: Sign in to the AWS Management Console in the us-east-1 (N. Virginia) region ➔ Open Amazon EC2 ➔ Navigate to Instances. Procedure: Launch two standard t3.micro instances named ec2-instance-1 and ec2-instance-2. Observe the status transitioning from Initializing to Running. Step 2: Inspect Default Instance Metadata Tags Action: Select ec2-instance-1 (i-02b440e03f77f9942) ➔ In the details pane below, switch to the Tags tab to audit active tags. Step 3: Configure Custom Metadata Tags via Manage Tags Action: In the Tags tab, click Manage tags ➔ Click Add new tag to establish standard key-value pairs: Key: Environment | Value: Test Key: Service | Value: YourService Key: Name | Value: ec2-instance-1 Key: Owner | Value: YourName Key: OS | Value: Amazon Linux Click Save to persist the configuration. Step 4: Filter Instances by Tag in the Management Console Action: In the EC2 Instances search bar, enter Owner = ➔ The console dynamically displays available values (YourName, Not tagged, All values). Select Owner = YourName to isolate workloads belonging to that owner. Section 2: Command-Line Tag Automation via AWS CLI Step 5: Provision IAM Access Key for CLI Authentication Action: Open the IAM service ➔ Navigate to Security credentials under user trangiabao ➔ Click Create access key ➔ Select Command Line Interface (CLI). Result: Save the .csv file containing the Access Key ID (AKIA_DEMO_SAMPLE_KEY_ID) and Secret access key. Step 6: Configure Local Workstation Environment Profile Action: Open Windows PowerShell ➔ Execute the configuration routine: aws configure Parameters Entered: AWS Access Key ID: AKIA_DEMO_SAMPLE_KEY_ID AWS Secret Access Key: DEMO_SECRET_KEY_SAMPLE_TEST_12345 Default region name: us-east-1 Default output format: json Step 7: Apply Tags Programmatically via CLI Action: Execute the aws ec2 create-tags command to attach Project: AWS to ec2-instance-2: aws ec2 create-tags --resources i-0abb0b1178954e0a4 --tags Key=Project,Value=AWS Step 8: Validate Tag Injection on the Management Console Action: Return to the web console and apply the filter Project = AWS. The interface displays ec2-instance-2 (i-0abb0b1178954e0a4), confirming programmatic tag assignment. Step 9: Multi-Tag Injection in a Single Command Invocation Action: Apply both Env: Test and Project: AWS tags in a single atomic command: aws ec2 create-tags --resources i-0abb0b1178954e0a4 --tags Key=Env,Value=Test Key=Project,Value=AWS Step 10: Provision Third Instance and Validate Fleet Status Action: Provision instance ec2-instance-3 (i-00ecbe56e33f40770) with tag Environment: Test via CLI. Verification: Confirm all three instances (ec2-instance-1, ec2-instance-2, ec2-instance-3) are operating in Running status in us-east-1a. Step 11: Advanced Tag Querying using CLI Filter Flags Action: Execute an instance descriptor query filtering on instances tagged Environment: Test: aws ec2 describe-instances --filters Name=tag:Environment,Values=Test Result: CLI outputs formatted JSON metadata covering instance configurations, security groups, and network interfaces for matched workloads. Section 3: Centralized Governance with AWS Resource Groups Step 12: Configure a Tag-Based Resource Group Action: Open the AWS Resource Groups console ➔ Click Create Resource Group. Group Parameters: Group type: Tag based Resource types: AWS::EC2::Instance Tags filter: Key: Environment | Value: Test Preview Group: Click Preview group resources. The query dynamically resolves the two target workloads: ec2-instance-1 (i-02b440e03f77f9942) and ec2-instance-3 (i-00ecbe56e33f40770). Step 13: Provision the Resource Group EnvTest Action: Set Group name: EnvTest ➔ Click Create group. Result: The console reports: The resource group "EnvTest" has been successfully created in the current region (us-east-1). The group is now ready for unified patch management, observability dashboards, and automation execution. 🛠️ Real-World Troubleshooting & Operational Insights: # Technical Symptom Root Cause Solution & Best Practice 1 Tag Case-Sensitivity Mismatch: Filtering by tag:environment returns empty results even though instances possess the tag. AWS Tags are strictly case-sensitive. Environment and environment represent distinct keys. Standardize organizational casing rules (e.g., PascalCase like Environment, Owner). Ensure CLI query strings exactly match stored metadata keys. 2 PowerShell Parameter Parsing Failure: CLI throws an Unknown options error when parsing complex filter arguments. PowerShell splits unquoted string parameters containing colons and equals signs incorrectly. Format filter parameters without internal spaces: Name=tag:KeyName,Values=ValueName or wrap arguments in single quotes '...'. 3 Tag Quota Limit Exception: Receiving TagLimitExceeded when appending additional tags. AWS enforces a maximum ceiling of 50 user-defined tags per resource. Implement lean tagging schemas. Periodically audit and remove obsolete temporary tags using the AWS Tag Editor. 4 Resource Group Regional Boundaries: A resource group in us-east-1 does not enumerate instances running in ap-southeast-1. Standard Resource Groups operate strictly within regional boundaries (Regional Scope). Create dedicated resource groups per target region or aggregate cross-region inventory using AWS Systems Manager Explorer. 5 IAM Permission Denied on Tagging: Receiving AccessDenied when executing aws ec2 create-tags. The IAM policy grants ec2:RunInstances but omits the ec2:CreateTags permission. Update the policy statement to explicitly allow ec2:CreateTags on arn:aws:ec2:*:*:instance/*. 🧹 Resource Cleanup: Delete Resource Group: Open AWS Resource Groups ➔ Select EnvTest ➔ Click Delete (Deleting a group does not affect underlying EC2 instances). Terminate EC2 Instances: Open Amazon EC2 ➔ Select all 3 instances (ec2-instance-1, ec2-instance-2, ec2-instance-3) ➔ Instance state ➔ Terminate instance. Deactivate CLI Credentials: Navigate to IAM ➔ User trangiabao ➔ Security credentials ➔ Deactivate or Delete the test Access Key.

title: Work with Amazon DynamoDB
content:
The Work with Amazon DynamoDB hands-on lab was conducted on Wednesday (14/10/2026) as part of Week 5. This document details the end-to-end implementation process across three operational methods: AWS Management Console, AWS CloudShell CLI, and Programmatic Automation with Python SDK (Boto3). 🔗 Workshop Source: Work with Amazon DynamoDB (Workshop 000060)
🎯 Lab Objectives: Master the NoSQL architecture of Amazon DynamoDB, comprehend partition distribution mechanisms using Partition Key (HASH), composite key strategies using Composite Primary Key (HASH + RANGE), and schema flexibility with Scalar/Document attribute types. Perform lifecycle management for the Music table via AWS Management Console: table creation, item insertion, in-place updates, conditional queries and full table scans, alongside configuring and querying a Global Secondary Index (GSI) named AlbumTitle-index. Leverage the command-line interface of AWS CloudShell: authenticate via IAM credentials, provision tables, perform atomic CRUD operations (put-item, get-item, update-item, query), attach a GSI via update-table, and understand the asynchronous Backfilling phase. Implement programmatic automation on Windows using Python 3 and Boto3 SDK: automated provisioning of the Movies table, item CRUD scripts, batch ingestion from a JSON payload (moviedata.json with 4,609 records), key-based queries, and filtered table scans (MoviesScan.py). Analyze and document 10 in-depth real-world troubleshooting scenarios: workshop documentation flag typos, IAM policy authorization, duplicate resource conflicts, hidden zero-width Unicode characters (\u200b), terminal CLI pager behavior, GSI backfilling locks, environment execution mismatches, and multi-region routing. 📊 Provisioned Resource Specifications: Resource Name / Identifier Attributes & Key Schema Throughput / Mode Region Purpose DynamoDB Table 1 Music Partition Key: Artist (S) Sort Key: SongTitle (S) Provisioned (RCU=10, WCU=5) us-east-1 Console & CloudShell CLI lab exercises Secondary Index AlbumTitle-index Partition Key: AlbumTitle (S) Projection: ALL Provisioned (RCU=10, WCU=5) us-east-1 Global Secondary Index for Music table DynamoDB Table 2 Movies Partition Key: year (N) Sort Key: title (S) Provisioned (RCU=10, WCU=10) ap-southeast-1 Python SDK (Boto3) lab automation IAM User AWS-FCAJ-DynamDB Attached Policy: AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess Programmatic CLI Access Global Dedicated identity for CLI and SDK access Dataset Payload moviedata.json 4,609 movie entries (3.7 MB), JSON format Parsed Floats to Decimal Local Benchmark dataset for query & scan routines SDK Environment Windows Workstation Python 3.14.5 + Boto3 1.43.114 CLI Default: ap-southeast-1 Local Host environment for Python test scripts 📋 Section 1: Managing DynamoDB via AWS Management Console Step 1: Accessing the Amazon DynamoDB Console Action: Sign in to the AWS Management Console and open the DynamoDB service dashboard. Purpose: Access the centralized control pane to monitor database capacity, active tables, and operational metrics. Step 2: Creating an IAM Access Key for Authentication Action: Navigate to IAM ➔ Users ➔ Select user AWS-FCAJ-DynamDB ➔ Security credentials tab ➔ Click Create access key ➔ Select Command Line Interface (CLI) ➔ Download the credentials .csv file containing the Access Key ID and Secret Access Key. Step 3: Creating the Music Table on Web Console Action: In the DynamoDB Console navigation sidebar, select Tables ➔ Click Create table. Configuration Parameters: Table name: Music Partition key: Artist (Data Type: String) Sort key: SongTitle (Data Type: String) Table settings: Select Default settings (Provisioned capacity mode, RCU=5, WCU=5, default KMS encryption). Action: Click Create table and monitor until the status turns to Active. Step 4: Writing the First Item to Music Table Action: Select table Music ➔ Click Explore items ➔ Click Create item. Attribute Entries: Artist (String): No One You Know SongTitle (String): Call Me Today Click Add new attribute ➔ String ➔ Name: AlbumTitle, Value: Somewhat Famous Click Add new attribute ➔ Number ➔ Name: Awards, Value: 1 Action: Click Create item to commit the record to storage. Step 5: Viewing and Scanning Stored Records Action: In Explore items, select the Music table and execute a Scan operation to list all persisted items. Verification: The view displays all assigned attributes for the newly inserted track. Step 6: Inspecting Item Attributes Action: Click on the record row for No One You Know to inspect the underlying document structure in Form or JSON format. Step 7: Updating Item Attributes in Place Action: Select the record, modify attribute values or add new fields, and click Save changes. Step 8: Querying Data by Primary Key Action: Under Explore items, toggle the execution mode from Scan to Query. Query Parameters: Partition key (Artist): Acme Band Sort key (SongTitle): Optional condition or left blank to fetch all tracks under this partition. Result: Ultra-low latency retrieval restricted exclusively to the target hash partition. Step 9: Creating a Global Secondary Index (GSI) Action: Open table Music ➔ Select the Indexes tab ➔ Click Create index. Index Configuration: Partition key: AlbumTitle (Type: String) Index name: AlbumTitle-index Attribute projections: All Action: Click Create index. The index status switches to Creating as the background Backfilling process begins. Step 10: Querying Stored Items via GSI Action: Return to Explore items ➔ Select Query ➔ Choose AlbumTitle-index from the target dropdown. Search Parameters: Partition key (AlbumTitle): Somewhat Famous Result: Returns matching tracks without requiring knowledge of the primary key’s partition key (Artist), demonstrating multi-dimensional query flexibility. 📋 Section 2: Command-Line Operations via AWS CloudShell Step 11: Launching AWS CloudShell Action: Click the CloudShell terminal icon on the top navigation bar of the AWS Console to open an authenticated Linux browser shell. Step 12: Configuring CLI Credentials in CloudShell Execution Command: aws configure Input Parameters: AWS Access Key ID: Provide Access Key for AWS-FCAJ-DynamDB. AWS Secret Access Key: Provide matching Secret Access Key. Default region name: us-east-1 Default output format: json Step 13: Creating Table Music via AWS CLI Execution Command: aws dynamodb create-table \ --table-name Music \ --attribute-definitions \ AttributeName=Artist,AttributeType=S \ AttributeName=SongTitle,AttributeType=S \ --key-schema \ AttributeName=Artist,KeyType=HASH \ AttributeName=SongTitle,KeyType=RANGE \ --provisioned-throughput \ ReadCapacityUnits=10,WriteCapacityUnits=5 \ --table-class STANDARD 💡 Trouble 1 & Resolution - Workshop Documentation Syntax Typo:
Issue: The original workshop instructions specified --provided-throughput, throwing: aws: [ERROR]: Unknown options: --provided-throughput, ReadCapacityUnits=10,WriteCapacityUnits=5. Root Cause: Standard AWS CLI v2 syntax mandates --provisioned-throughput. Resolution: Replaced flag with --provisioned-throughput ReadCapacityUnits=10,WriteCapacityUnits=5. 💡 Trouble 2 & Resolution - Missing IAM Permissions (AccessDeniedException):
Issue: Call denied with User: .../AWS-FCAJ-DynamDB is not authorized to perform: dynamodb:CreateTable because no identity-based policy allows.... Root Cause: The IAM User lacked permissions policies for DynamoDB APIs. Resolution: Attached managed policy AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess directly to user AWS-FCAJ-DynamDB via IAM Console. 💡 Trouble 3 & Resolution - Resource Name Collision (ResourceInUseException):
Issue: Output indicated: Table already exists: Music. Root Cause: Table Music had already been created in Section 1 via Web Console in the identical region (us-east-1). Resolution: Executed describe-table to confirm ACTIVE state and proceeded directly to subsequent data manipulation steps. Step 14: Verifying Table Status Execution Command: aws dynamodb describe-table --table-name Music | grep TableStatus Output: Returned "TableStatus": "ACTIVE". Step 15: Ingesting an Item via put-item Execution Command: aws dynamodb put-item \ --table-name Music \ --item '{ "Artist": {"S": "No One You Know"}, "SongTitle": {"S": "Call Me Today"}, "AlbumTitle": {"S": "Somewhat Famous"}, "Awards": {"N": "1"} }' Step 16: Ingesting Additional Items for Acme Band Action: Repeated put-item commands for tracks Happy Day (Awards: 10, Album: Songs About Life) and PartiQL Rocks (Awards: 8, Album: Another Album Title). Step 17: Fetching a Single Item via get-item Execution Command: aws dynamodb get-item \ --table-name Music \ --key '{ "Artist": {"S": "Acme Band"}, "SongTitle": {"S": "Happy Day"} }' Step 18: Updating Attributes via update-item Execution Command: aws dynamodb update-item \ --table-name Music \ --key '{ "Artist": {"S": "Acme Band"}, "SongTitle": {"S": "Happy Day"} }' \ --update-expression "SET AlbumTitle = :a" \ --expression-attribute-values '{":a": {"S": "Updated Album Title"}}' \ --return-values ALL_NEW Step 19: Confirming Updated Attributes Result: Output returned ReturnValues indicating AlbumTitle was successfully updated to "Updated Album Title". Step 20: Querying Items with query Execution Command: aws dynamodb query \ --table-name Music \ --key-condition-expression "Artist = :name" \ --expression-attribute-values '{":name":{"S":"Acme Band"}}' 💡 Trouble 4 & Resolution - Hidden Zero-Width Unicode Characters (\u200b):
Issue: Command parsing failed with: Error parsing parameter '--expression-attribute-values': Expected: '=', received: '' for input: {":name"...}. Root Cause: Copying from the workshop web page pulled two invisible Zero-Width Space characters (\u200b\u200b) directly behind --expression-attribute-values, breaking CLI argument interpretation. Resolution: Stripped hidden unicode bytes and reconstructed with standard ASCII spaces. Step 21: Attaching a Global Secondary Index via update-table Execution Command: aws dynamodb update-table \ --table-name Music \ --attribute-definitions AttributeName=AlbumTitle,AttributeType=S \ --global-secondary-index-updates \ "[{\"Create\":{\"IndexName\": \"AlbumTitle-index\",\"KeySchema\":[{\"AttributeName\":\"AlbumTitle\",\"KeyType\": \"HASH\"}], \ \"ProvisionedThroughput\": {\"ReadCapacityUnits\": 10, \"WriteCapacityUnits\": 5 },\"Projection\":{\"ProjectionType\":\"ALL\"}}}]" 💡 Trouble 5 & Resolution - Terminal Pager Auto-Exit Behavior:
Issue: After execution, the terminal momentarily flashed JSON output and immediately exited back to the prompt ~ $. Root Cause: AWS CLI pipes voluminous responses to the less pager by default. Pressing q or scrolling to EOF closes the pager. The underlying GSI provisioning continues normally in the background. Resolution: Executed export AWS_PAGER="" to disable the pager and print JSON directly to standard output. Step 22: Querying the GSI via query Execution Command: aws dynamodb query \ --table-name Music \ --index-name AlbumTitle-index \ --key-condition-expression "AlbumTitle = :name" \ --expression-attribute-values '{":name":{"S":"Somewhat Famous"}}' 💡 Trouble 6 & Resolution - Querying a Backfilling Index:
Issue: Threw: ValidationException: Cannot read from backfilling global secondary index: AlbumTitle-index. Root Cause: New GSIs created on populated tables undergo asynchronous data copying (Backfilling). Reads are disallowed while IndexStatus is CREATING. Resolution: Polled describe-table until IndexStatus transitioned to ACTIVE before re-issuing query. 📋 Section 3: Programmatic Automation with Python SDK (Boto3) Step 23: Setting up Python & Boto3 Environment on Windows Action: Open Command Prompt (cmd.exe), verify Python installation, install Boto3, and configure credentials: python --version pip install boto3 aws configure Step 24: Provisioning Table Movies with MoviesCreateTable.py File: MoviesCreateTable.py Script Code: import boto3 def create_movie_table(dynamodb=None): dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb') table = dynamodb.create_table( TableName='Movies', KeySchema=[ {'AttributeName': 'year', 'KeyType': 'HASH'}, # Partition key {'AttributeName': 'title', 'KeyType': 'RANGE'} # Sort key ], AttributeDefinitions=[ {'AttributeName': 'year', 'AttributeType': 'N'}, {'AttributeName': 'title', 'AttributeType': 'S'} ], ProvisionedThroughput={ 'ReadCapacityUnits': 10, 'WriteCapacityUnits': 10 } ) return table if __name__ == '__main__': movie_table = create_movie_table() print("Table status:", movie_table.table_status) Execution: cd /d D:\AWS\template_AWS\fcj-workshop-template-main python MoviesCreateTable.py 💡 Trouble 7 & Resolution - Pasting Raw Python Code into Windows CMD:
Issue: Directly pasting Python statements into cmd.exe triggered multiple errors: 'import' is not recognized as an internal or external command. Root Cause: Windows CMD is a command-line shell, not an interactive Python interpreter. Resolution: Saved source code into dedicated .py files and invoked them using python <file>.py. 💡 Trouble 8 & Resolution - Default Working Directory at System32:
Issue: Execution yielded: can't open file 'C:\Windows\System32\MoviesCreateTable.py': No such file or directory. Root Cause: CMD opened inside protected system directories rather than the project workspace. Resolution: Changed working directory using: cd /d D:\AWS\template_AWS\fcj-workshop-template-main. Step 25: Inserting Movies with MoviesItemOps01.py File: MoviesItemOps01.py Script Code: from pprint import pprint import boto3 def put_movie(title, year, plot, rating, dynamodb=None): dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb') table = dynamodb.Table('Movies') response = table.put_item( Item={ 'year': year, 'title': title, 'info': {'plot': plot, 'rating': rating} } ) return response if __name__ == '__main__': movie_resp = put_movie("The Big New Movie", 2015, "Nothing happens at all.", 0) print("Put movie succeeded:") pprint(movie_resp, sort_dicts=False) Execution Command: python MoviesItemOps01.py Result: Returned HTTP 200 indicating successful write. Step 26: Reading Stored Movies with MoviesItemOps02.py File: MoviesItemOps02.py Script Code: from pprint import pprint import boto3 from botocore.exceptions import ClientError def get_movie(title, year, dynamodb=None): dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb') table = dynamodb.Table('Movies') try: response = table.get_item(Key={'year': year, 'title': title}) except ClientError as e: print(e.response['Error']['Message']) else: return response['Item'] if __name__ == '__main__': movie = get_movie("The Big New Movie", 2015) if movie: print("Get movie succeeded:") pprint(movie, sort_dicts=False) Execution Command: python MoviesItemOps02.py Step 27: Updating Records with MoviesItemOps03.py File: MoviesItemOps03.py Script Code: from decimal import Decimal from pprint import pprint import boto3 def update_movie(title, year, rating, plot, actors, dynamodb=None): dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb') table = dynamodb.Table('Movies') response = table.update_item( Key={'year': year, 'title': title}, UpdateExpression="set info.rating=:r, info.plot=:p, info.actors=:a", ExpressionAttributeValues={ ':r': Decimal(str(rating)), ':p': plot, ':a': actors }, ReturnValues="UPDATED_NEW" ) return response if __name__ == '__main__': update_response = update_movie( "The Big New Movie", 2015, 5.5, "Everything happens all at once.", ["Larry", "Moe", "Curly"]) print("Update movie succeeded:") pprint(update_response, sort_dicts=False) Execution Command: python MoviesItemOps03.py Step 28: Conditional Deletion with MoviesItemOps04.py File: MoviesItemOps04.py Script Code: from decimal import Decimal from pprint import pprint import boto3 from botocore.exceptions import ClientError def delete_underrated_movie(title, year, rating, dynamodb=None): dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb') table = dynamodb.Table('Movies') try: response = table.delete_item(Key={'year': year, 'title': title}) except ClientError as e: if e.response['Error']['Code'] == "ConditionalCheckFailedException": print(e.response['Error']['Message']) else: raise else: return response if __name__ == '__main__': print("Attempting a conditional delete...") delete_response = delete_underrated_movie("The Big New Movie", 2015, 5) if delete_response: print("Delete movie succeeded:") pprint(delete_response, sort_dicts=False) Execution Command: python MoviesItemOps04.py Step 29: Ingesting Bulk Dataset with MoviesLoadData.py Dataset: Extracted moviedata.json (3.7MB, 4,609 entries) from moviedata.zip. File: MoviesLoadData.py Script Code: from decimal import Decimal import json import boto3 def load_movies(movies, dynamodb=None): dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb') table = dynamodb.Table('Movies') for movie in movies: year = int(movie['year']) title = movie['title'] print("Adding movie:", year, title) table.put_item(Item=movie) if __name__ == '__main__': with open("moviedata.json") as json_file: movie_list = json.load(json_file, parse_float=Decimal) load_movies(movie_list) Execution Command: python MoviesLoadData.py 💡 Trouble 9 & Resolution - Large Dataset Ingestion Throughput:
With 4,609 records, standard iterative put_item operations may take several minutes depending on provisioned WCU. Ingestion can be safely interrupted (Ctrl + C) after seeding sufficient benchmark data for query verification. Step 30: Querying Released Movies for 1985 with MoviesQuery01.py File: MoviesQuery01.py Script Code: import boto3 from boto3.dynamodb.conditions import Key def query_movies(year, dynamodb=None): dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb') table = dynamodb.Table('Movies') response = table.query( KeyConditionExpression=Key('year').eq(year) ) return response['Items'] if __name__ == '__main__': query_year = 1985 print(f"Movies from {query_year}") movies = query_movies(query_year) for movie in movies: print(movie['year'], ":", movie['title']) Execution Command: python MoviesQuery01.py Output: Fetched all 1985 classics including Back to the Future, Rambo: First Blood Part II, Rocky IV, The Breakfast Club… Step 31: Full Table Scan with Filters using MoviesScan.py File: MoviesScan.py Script Code: from pprint import pprint import boto3 from boto3.dynamodb.conditions import Key def scan_movies(year_range, display_movies, dynamodb=None): dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb') table = dynamodb.Table('Movies') scan_kwargs = { 'FilterExpression': Key('year').between(*year_range), 'ProjectionExpression': "#yr, title, info.rating", 'ExpressionAttributeNames': {"#yr": "year"} } done = False start_key = None while not done: if start_key: scan_kwargs['ExclusiveStartKey'] = start_key response = table.scan(**scan_kwargs) display_movies(response.get('Items', [])) start_key = response.get('LastEvaluatedKey', None) done = start_key is None if __name__ == '__main__': def print_movies(movies): for movie in movies: print(f"\n{movie['year']} : {movie['title']}") pprint(movie['info']) query_range = (1950, 1959) print(f"Scanning for movies released from {query_range[0]} to {query_range[1]}...") scan_movies(query_range, print_movies) Execution Command: python MoviesScan.py Step 32: Decommissioning the Movies Table with MoviesDeleteTable.py File: MoviesDeleteTable.py Script Code: import boto3 def delete_movie_table(dynamodb=None): dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb') table = dynamodb.Table('Movies') table.delete() if __name__ == '__main__': delete_movie_table() print("Movies table deleted.") Execution Command: python MoviesDeleteTable.py 📋 Section 4: Resource Cleanup & Summary of Troubles 💡 Trouble 10 & Resolution - Cross-Region Deletion Failure (ResourceNotFoundException):
Issue: CloudShell command aws dynamodb delete-table --table-name Music threw: Requested resource not found: Table: Music not found. Root Cause: Default CloudShell region pointed to ap-southeast-1 (Singapore) whereas table Music was provisioned in us-east-1 (N. Virginia), or was previously dropped via Web Console. Resolution: Target explicit region by appending --region us-east-1. 💡 Summary Table of 10 Real-World Troubleshooting Cases: # Technical Difficulty Root Cause Standardized Resolution 1 Flag parsing error --provided-throughput Typographical error in upstream workshop documentation. Replaced with standard AWS CLI flag: --provisioned-throughput. 2 AccessDeniedException on table creation IAM User AWS-FCAJ-DynamDB lacked DynamoDB policies. Attached managed policy AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess via IAM Console. 3 ResourceInUseException: Table already exists Duplicate table Music already provisioned in same region. Inspected via describe-table and reused existing active table. 4 Expected: '=', received: '' during query Embedded zero-width space unicode characters (\u200b). Stripped unicode bytes and applied clean ASCII command string. 5 Terminal prompt auto-exit after update AWS CLI v2 automatically activates less pager for large JSON. Pressed q to dismiss or ran export AWS_PAGER="" to disable pager. 6 Cannot read from backfilling GSI Querying index while asynchronous data backfill is in flight. Monitored IndexStatus via describe-table until reaching ACTIVE. 7 'import' is not recognized in Windows CMD Directly pasting Python script statements into Windows shell. Persisted code into dedicated .py files and invoked via python <file>.py. 8 No such file or directory at System32 CMD launched inside Windows system directory by default. Shifted working directory: cd /d D:\AWS\template_AWS\fcj-workshop-template-main. 9 Slow ingestion of 4,609 sample records Large JSON payload throttled by provisioned WCU limit. Ingested sufficient benchmark partition records before running queries. 10 Table: Music not found on table deletion Region mismatch between CLI configuration (ap-southeast-1) and table (us-east-1). Appended explicit region parameter: aws dynamodb delete-table --region us-east-1.

title: Auto Scaling with EC2 Auto Scaling
content:
The Auto Scaling with EC2 Auto Scaling (Scaling Applications with EC2 Auto Scaling) hands-on lab was conducted on Wednesday (07/10/2026) during Week 4. This page delivers a detailed step-by-step walkthrough covering explicit parameters, stress testing commands, troubleshooting resolutions, and all 44 verification screenshots. 🔗 Lab Reference Material: Triển khai ứng dụng FCAJ Management với Auto Scaling Group
🎯 Lab Objectives: Understand the core design principles of Scalable & Highly Available Architecture on AWS. Package a functional application server into a reusable Custom AMI. Construct a standardized Launch Template defining automated compute specifications. Deploy an Application Load Balancer (ALB) paired with a Target Group for balanced traffic distribution. Configure an Auto Scaling Group (ASG) with Dynamic Scaling Policies driven by CloudWatch CPU metrics. Execute a synthetic Stress Test to validate automated Scale Out and Scale In lifecycle behaviors. Execute a complete teardown procedure to decommission all provisioned resources and prevent unintended costs. 📊 Provisioned Resource Specifications: Resource Name / Identifier Configuration & Detailed Specs Address / Ports Notes Custom AMI fcaj-app-ami Packaged sample Node.js server + application code AMI ID: ami-0... Master golden image for fleet instances Launch Template fcaj-launch-template t2.micro, Amazon Linux, SG: Ports 80/3000 Version 1 Automates instance provisioning Target Group fcaj-tg Target Type: Instance, Protocol: HTTP (Port 80) Health Check: / Manages target registration and health checks Load Balancer fcaj-alb Application Load Balancer, Multi-AZ Subnets DNS Name of ALB Central ingress traffic gateway Auto Scaling Group fcaj-asg Min: 1, Desired: 1, Max: 3 instances Distributed across 2 Availability Zones Auto-manages fleet capacity Scaling Policy TargetTracking-CPU Metric: Average CPU Utilization > 50% Warmup: 300s Automatically triggers Scale Out under load 🚀 Step-by-Step Implementation & Screenshot Gallery: Step 1: Create Custom AMI from Baseline EC2 Instance Action / Navigation: In the Amazon EC2 console ➔ Navigate to Instances ➔ Select the running golden application instance ➔ Click Actions ➔ Image and templates ➔ Click Create image. Purpose: Package the operating system, code dependencies, and runtime environment into an immutable golden image for automated fleet scaling. 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Troubleshooting at Step 1:
By default, creating an AMI causes AWS to temporarily reboot the instance to ensure filesystem synchronization. If uninterrupted uptime is strictly required, the “No reboot” option can be checked; however, allowing reboot is strongly advised to guarantee image data integrity.
Step 2: Configure Name and Storage Volumes for Custom AMI Action / Navigation: Fill in the image configuration parameters. Configuration Parameters: Image name: fcaj-app-ami Image description: Custom AMI for FCAJ Management Application with Node.js Instance volumes: 1x Root EBS volume (8 GiB, General Purpose SSD gp2) Next Action: Click Create image. Step 3: Monitor AMI Generation Status Action / Navigation: In the EC2 navigation sidebar, navigate to Images ➔ AMIs. Observation: The AMI fcaj-app-ami begins block-level copying with initial status showing pending. Step 4: Verify AMI Available Status Action / Navigation: Wait 3 to 5 minutes and refresh the AMIs console. Observation: Status transitions to available, confirming readiness for Launch Template integration. Step 5: Inspect AMI Configuration Details & Underlying Snapshot Action / Navigation: Select fcaj-app-ami and review the Details pane. Details Observed: An associated Snapshot ID is linked under Elastic Block Store, virtualization type hvm, architecture x86_64. Step 6: Create Target Group for Application Load Balancer Action / Navigation: In the EC2 sidebar, select Target Groups ➔ Click Create target group. Configuration Parameters: Target type: Instances Target group name: fcaj-tg Protocol / Port: HTTP : 80 VPC: Select Default VPC or Workshop VPC Health checks: Protocol HTTP, Path / Next Action: Click Next ➔ Click Create target group (manual target registration is bypassed because ASG handles this automatically). Step 7: Create Application Load Balancer (fcaj-alb) Action / Navigation: Select Load Balancers ➔ Click Create load balancer ➔ Select Application Load Balancer. Configuration Parameters: Load balancer name: fcaj-alb Scheme: Internet-facing IP address type: IPv4 Network mapping: Select VPC and at least two public Availability Zones / Subnets Security groups: Attach a Security Group permitting Inbound Port 80 (HTTP) from 0.0.0.0/0 Listeners and routing: Port 80 (HTTP) ➔ Forward to fcaj-tg Next Action: Scroll down and click Create load balancer. 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Troubleshooting at Step 7:
The ALB Security Group must allow open public HTTP traffic (0.0.0.0/0), but backend EC2 instances should strictly restrict incoming port 80 traffic to the ALB Security Group ID only. This ensures all traffic is properly filtered and inspected by the load balancer.
Step 8: Initiate Launch Template Creation Action / Navigation: In the EC2 sidebar, click Launch Templates ➔ Click Create launch template. Purpose: Define compute specifications, security boundaries, and bootstrap scripts for automated ASG provisioning. Step 9: Configure Launch Template Metadata and Version Action / Navigation: Populate identity fields for the template. Configuration Parameters: Launch template name: fcaj-launch-template Template version description: Initial version for FCAJ ASG Auto Scaling guidance: Check “Provide guidance to help me set up a template that I can use with EC2 Auto Scaling”. Step 10: Select Custom AMI Source (fcaj-app-ami) Action / Navigation: Under Application and OS Images (Amazon Machine Image) ➔ Click My AMIs ➔ Select Owned by me. Selection: Select fcaj-app-ami created in Step 4. Step 11: Specify Instance Type Action / Navigation: Under Instance type, pick the Free-Tier eligible size. Configuration: t2.micro (1 vCPU, 1 GiB Memory). Step 12: Configure SSH Authentication Key Pair Action / Navigation: Under Key pair (login), specify key settings. Configuration: Select your pre-existing Key Pair or select Don't include in launch template if SSH direct access is not required. Step 13: Configure Network Settings & Security Group Action / Navigation: Under Network settings, configure firewall associations. Configuration Parameters: Subnet: Don't include in launch template (allowing ASG to distribute instances dynamically across subnets) Firewall (Security groups): Choose Select existing security group ➔ Select the SG permitting HTTP traffic from the ALB. Step 14: Configure Storage Volumes (EBS) Action / Navigation: Under Configure storage, retain golden AMI disk defaults. Configuration Parameters: 1x 8 GiB General Purpose SSD (gp2), Delete on termination: Yes. Step 15: Configure Advanced Details & User Data Bootstrap Script Action / Navigation: Expand Advanced details, scroll to User data. Bootstrap Script: #!/bin/bash # Ensure application server starts on boot cd /home/ec2-user/fcaj-app || cd /var/www/html npm start || systemctl restart httpd Step 16: Verify Successful Launch Template Creation Action / Navigation: Click Create launch template. Observation: A confirmation screen verifies fcaj-launch-template has been successfully created as Version 1. Step 17: Initiate Auto Scaling Group Creation (fcaj-asg) Action / Navigation: In the EC2 sidebar, select Auto Scaling Groups ➔ Click Create Auto Scaling group. Configuration Parameters: Auto Scaling group name: fcaj-asg Launch template: Select fcaj-launch-template (Version Default (1)) Next Action: Click Next. Step 18: Select Network VPC and Multi-AZ Subnets Action / Navigation: On the Choose instance launch options step. Configuration Parameters: VPC: Select the workshop VPC Availability Zones and subnets: Select at least 2 Subnets across distinct AZs (e.g., ap-southeast-1a and ap-southeast-1b) for High Availability. Next Action: Click Next. Step 19: Attach ALB Target Group & Enable ELB Health Checks Action / Navigation: On the Configure advanced options step. Configuration Parameters: Load balancing: Choose Attach to an existing load balancer ➔ Select fcaj-tg. Health checks: Check Turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks. Health check grace period: 300 seconds. Next Action: Click Next. 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Troubleshooting at Step 19:
Without ELB health checks enabled, ASG only checks hypervisor status (EC2 status checks), missing cases where the web application crashes. Enabling ELB health checks ensures unresponsive instances are automatically terminated and replaced. Keep the grace period at 300 seconds so new instances have time to boot before health evaluation begins.
Step 20: Configure Group Size Capacities (Min, Desired, Max) Action / Navigation: On the Configure group size and scaling policies step. Configuration Parameters: Desired capacity: 1 Minimum capacity: 1 Maximum capacity: 3 Scaling policies: Select None temporarily (configured in Step 28). Next Action: Advance through Notifications and Tags by clicking Next. Step 21: Review ASG Configuration and Finalize Provisioning Action / Navigation: In the Review step, audit Launch Template, network mappings, and capacity constraints. Next Action: Click Create Auto Scaling group. Step 22: ASG Auto-Spawns Initial EC2 Instance Action / Navigation: Select fcaj-asg ➔ Navigate to the Activity tab. Observation: The activity log records Launching a new EC2 instance to satisfy Desired capacity = 1. Step 23: Validate InService Lifecycle State Action / Navigation: Click the Instance management tab within fcaj-asg. Observation: The newly provisioned instance displays Health status Healthy and Lifecycle state InService. Step 24: Verify Target Group Healthy State Action / Navigation: Return to Target Groups ➔ Select fcaj-tg ➔ Inspect the Targets tab. Observation: The instance registered by ASG shows health check status as healthy on port 80. Step 25: Access Application via ALB Public DNS Name Action / Navigation: Navigate to Load Balancers, copy the DNS name of fcaj-alb ➔ Open a web browser and navigate to http://<ALB-DNS-Name>. Result: Traffic is successfully routed through the load balancer to the active backend instance. Step 26: Authenticate into FCAJ Management Application Action / Navigation: Enter credentials on the application login interface to verify end-to-end functionality. Configuration Parameters: Username: admin Password: [Application default password] Next Action: Click Sign In. Step 27: Verify Operational Dashboard Status Action / Navigation: Inspect navigation elements upon successful authentication. Result: Application administrative dashboard loads reliably via ALB routing. Step 28: Configure Dynamic Scaling Policy on CPU Threshold Action / Navigation: In fcaj-asg details ➔ Select Automatic scaling tab ➔ Under Dynamic scaling policies, click Create dynamic scaling policy. Configuration Parameters: Policy type: Target tracking scaling Scaling policy name: TargetTracking-CPU Step 29: Define 50% Average CPU Utilization Target Action / Navigation: Configure Target Tracking parameters. Configuration Parameters: Metric type: Average CPU utilization Target value: 50 (%) Instance warmup: 300 seconds Next Action: Click Create. Step 30: Verify CloudWatch Alarms Triggered by Policy Action / Navigation: Open the CloudWatch console ➔ Select Alarms. Observation: Two alarms are generated automatically: One detecting CPU > 50% (triggers Scale Out) and one detecting CPU < 35% (triggers Scale In). Step 31: Execute Synthetic CPU Stress Test via SSH Action / Navigation: SSH into the running EC2 instance and execute the stress utility. Commands Executed: # Install stress utility sudo amazon-linux-extras install epel -y || sudo dnf install -y epel-release sudo yum install -y stress # Generate 100% load on 2 CPU cores for 600 seconds stress --cpu 2 --timeout 600s 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Troubleshooting at Step 31:
Standard CloudWatch metrics evaluate on 5-minute averages. Ensure the stress duration is maintained for at least 600 seconds (10 minutes), or enable Detailed Monitoring on the instance to guarantee swift alarm state changes.
Step 32: Observe CPU Utilization Spike on CloudWatch Action / Navigation: Open the CloudWatch metric graph for CPUUtilization. Observation: CPU load surges sharply from baseline (~1%) to nearly 100%, breaching the 50% target threshold. Step 33: CloudWatch Alarm Fires Scale Out Event Action / Navigation: Return to the Activity tab in fcaj-asg. Observation: The alarm changes state to In alarm, triggering Launching a new EC2 instance to balance the target metric. Step 34: Fleet Expands & Balances Workload Seamlessly Action / Navigation: Inspect the Instance management tab and Target Groups. Result: Capacity scales up from 1 to 2 (up to 3 per Max size configuration), both registering as InService and Healthy, dividing traffic and stabilizing the workload. Step 35: Resource Cleanup Step 1 - Delete Auto Scaling Group Action / Navigation: After lab completion, navigate to Auto Scaling Groups ➔ Select fcaj-asg ➔ Click Actions ➔ Click Delete. Step 36: Confirm Deletion and Await Instance Termination Action / Navigation: Type the confirmation keyword. Parameter: Enter delete ➔ Click Delete. All fleet instances managed by ASG terminate automatically. Step 37: Verify All EC2 Fleet Instances Terminated Action / Navigation: In the EC2 console, review Instances. Observation: Fleet instances transition to Terminated, shutting down compute billing. Step 38: Resource Cleanup Step 2 - Delete Application Load Balancer Action / Navigation: In the sidebar, select Load Balancers ➔ Select fcaj-alb ➔ Click Actions ➔ Click Delete load balancer ➔ Confirm Delete. Step 39: Delete Target Group (fcaj-tg) Action / Navigation: Navigate to Target Groups ➔ Select fcaj-tg ➔ Click Actions ➔ Click Delete. Step 40: Resource Cleanup Step 3 - Delete Launch Template Action / Navigation: Open Launch Templates ➔ Select fcaj-launch-template ➔ Click Actions ➔ Click Delete template. Step 41: Confirm Permanent Launch Template Deletion Action / Navigation: In the prompt, type Delete ➔ Click Delete. Step 42: Resource Cleanup Step 4 - Deregister Custom AMI Action / Navigation: Navigate to AMIs ➔ Select fcaj-app-ami ➔ Click Actions ➔ Click Deregister AMI ➔ Confirm deregistration. Step 43: Locate Associated EBS Snapshot of Deregistered AMI Action / Navigation: In the sidebar, open Elastic Block Store ➔ Snapshots ➔ Identify the snapshot referencing the deregistered AMI ID. Step 44: Permanently Delete EBS Snapshot to Prevent Storage Charges Action / Navigation: Select the snapshot ➔ Click Actions ➔ Click Delete snapshot ➔ Confirm Delete. Result: All workshop resources are cleanly expunged, eliminating residual cloud storage costs. 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Troubleshooting at Step 44:
Deregistering an AMI does not delete its underlying EBS snapshot. The snapshot remains in AWS storage and incurs monthly charges unless explicitly deleted. Always inspect the Snapshots console after deregistering AMIs.
📝 Summary & Key Takeaways: Self-Healing Architecture: EC2 Auto Scaling continuously evaluates ELB health checks, immediately terminating and replacing unresponsive instances without requiring operational intervention. Dynamic Cost Efficiency: Elastic scaling dynamically aligns compute consumption with real-time demand, automatically shedding surplus instances during low-traffic periods. Stateless Tier Best Practice: Applications deployed within Auto Scaling Groups should maintain a stateless architecture, offloading state to managed databases (RDS) and distributed caching tiers (ElastiCache).

Three-Tier Serverless Web Architecture: Mastered decoupled serverless patterns: Client-side single-page applications hosted on Amazon S3 ➔ Business logic execution via Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda ➔ Persistent low-latency data storage on Amazon DynamoDB. Identity Lifecycle Governance with Amazon Cognito: Configured Cognito User Pools: Managed user registration, login authentication, email OTP verification, password resets, and Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA). Configured Cognito Identity Pools: Enabled federated identity mapping, vending short-lived temporary AWS STS credentials granting authenticated end-users direct access to scoped AWS resources (such as uploading user profile photos to dedicated S3 user prefixes). Infrastructure as Code via AWS SAM (Serverless Application Model): Authored concise declarative template.yaml manifests defining Lambda handlers, DynamoDB tables, and API routes, automating compilation and deployment via sam build and sam deploy. Figure 1.3.1: Serverless event-driven architecture orchestrating AWS Lambda and downstream managed services.
Figure 1.3.2: Centralized user authentication and granular authorization model via Amazon Cognito and IAM Roles.
Encountered Challenges & Solutions: API Gateway Token Validation Rejections: Client requests passing Cognito JWT tokens received HTTP 401 Unauthorized. Root cause: The HTTP Authorization request header omitted the mandatory Bearer prefix. Solution: Standardized the client request interceptor to transmit headers strictly formatted as Bearer <id_token>. 📌 Tuesday (09/29/2026) - Enterprise Container Services & Kubernetes What did we learn today? Microservices Decomposition with Amazon ECS Fargate: Explored decomposing legacy monolithic architectures into decoupled service tasks (Authentication, Product Catalog, Order Processing), containerizing workloads with Docker, and running on serverless AWS Fargate infrastructure with independent scaling policies. Managed Kubernetes on Amazon EKS: Evaluated industrial Kubernetes primitives: Pods, Services, Deployments, ReplicaSets, and Ingress controllers. Analyzed how EKS manages a highly available multi-AZ control plane, ensuring open-standard container workload portability without proprietary vendor lock-in. Enterprise Hybrid Platforms with ROSA: Evaluated Red Hat OpenShift on AWS (ROSA), delivering a unified, managed OpenShift experience that bridges on-premises enterprise data centers with public cloud infrastructure. Figure 1.3.3: Multi-tier microservices container architecture operating on Amazon ECS backed by AWS Fargate.
Encountered Challenges & Solutions: Container Orchestration Platform Selection: Evaluated decision criteria between ECS and EKS. Takeaway: Adopt Amazon ECS Fargate when teams prioritize operational simplicity, tight AWS service integration, and lower administrative overhead; Adopt Amazon EKS when organizations maintain existing Kubernetes operational expertise, require complex Helm ecosystem tooling, or mandate multi-cloud deployment parity. 📌 Wednesday (09/30/2026) - Cloud Data Lakes & Business Intelligence What did we learn today? Modern Data Lake Architectural Principles: Analyzed the benefits of breaking data silos by consolidating structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data into an immutable Amazon S3 lake, decoupling storage capacity from analytical compute engines. Automated Data Cataloging with AWS Glue: Configured Glue Crawlers to scan S3 raw log directories, automatically inferring record schemas and registering partition metadata within the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Distributed SQL Queries & Visual Analytics: Executed serverless ANSI SQL queries against raw datasets via Amazon Athena without managing relational database servers, piping query results directly into Amazon QuickSight to render interactive operational charts. Figure 1.3.4: End-to-end data lake pipeline from ingestion and S3 storage to Glue cataloging and QuickSight visualization.
Encountered Challenges & Solutions: Escalating Query Costs on Raw CSV Datasets: Running repeated SELECT queries across multi-gigabyte uncompressed CSV files resulted in full-table scans. Solution: Applied the best practice of transforming data into columnar Apache Parquet format with Snappy compression and chronological partitioning, reducing scanned data volumes by over 90%. 📌 Thursday (10/01/2026) - Hands-On Amazon RDS Deployment 👉 Detailed Hands-on Report: The complete step-by-step configuration, VPC topologies, chained security groups, EC2 web client scripts, manual snapshots, and 10 verifiable screenshots are documented in the dedicated sub-page: 1.3.1. Hands-On Amazon RDS Deployment.
What did we learn today? Secure Two-Tier Network Architecture: Deployed VPC rds-vpc (10.0.0.0/16) spanning 4 subnets across 2 Availability Zones: 2 Public Subnets hosting EC2 Web Servers and 2 Private Subnets dedicated strictly to Amazon RDS. Ensured database instances possess zero public IP addresses and zero default internet routes, eliminating external attack vectors. Security Group Chaining: Hardened network perimeters by configuring the database security group rds-sg to authorize inbound MySQL traffic (port 3306) exclusively from the security group ID of the web server ec2-sg (sg-0cec4d0fbfc6d4c41), eliminating static IP whitelisting. High Availability with Amazon RDS Multi-AZ: Provisioned a DB Subnet Group rds-subnet-group containing private subnets across us-east-1a and us-east-1b. Launched a MySQL Community database (db.m5.large) with Multi-AZ replication. AWS maintains a primary instance while synchronously replicating storage blocks to an active standby instance in the secondary zone. In the event of an infrastructure outage, automated failover executes in under 60 seconds without client DNS reconfiguration. Disaster Recovery via Point-in-Time Recovery & Snapshots: Mastered continuous automated daily backups supporting Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) to any second within the retention window. Executed an explicit Manual Snapshot, stored durably in S3, and executed a complete restore drill to provision an independent replacement instance from the snapshot. Figure 1.3.5: Secure Two-Tier architecture separating EC2 Web Servers from private Amazon RDS database clusters.
Figure 1.3.6: Amazon RDS MySQL Multi-AZ database cluster in available status.
Encountered Challenges & Solutions: EC2 Client Connection Timeouts to Database Endpoint: Executing mysql -h <rds-endpoint> -u admin -p timed out. Root cause: The EC2 instance was assigned a default security group instead of ec2-sg, failing the security group chaining rule. Solution: Attached ec2-sg to the web instance, immediately enabling successful client database handshakes. 📌 Friday (10/02/2026) - Week 3 Review, Worklog Finalization & Proposal Submission What did we learn today? Foundational Milestone Synthesis: Completed a holistic review of the 3-week foundation: Core infrastructure (IAM, VPC, EC2, S3) ➔ Well-Architected governance (Lambda, KMS, WAF, Fargate, Savings Plans) ➔ Application modernization, containers, analytics, and relational database engineering with Amazon RDS Multi-AZ. Bilingual Worklog Consolidation: Finalized the standalone hands-on report 1.3.1. Hands-On Amazon RDS Deployment, validating 10 architectural diagrams, configuration tables, and terminal execution evidence.
