title: Testing Interface Endpoint Connectivity
content:
1. Retrieve the Regional DNS Name of the S3 Interface Endpoint In the Amazon VPC Management Console, select Endpoints. Select the interface endpoint created in section 5.4.2: s3-interface-endpoint ➔ View the Details tab. Locate the DNS names section and copy the Regional DNS name (the top record formatted as vpce-xxxx-xxxx.s3.us-east-1.vpce.amazonaws.com) into your local text editor. 2. Establish Session Manager Shell to Simulated On-Premises Host Navigate to AWS Systems Manager Console ➔ Select Session Manager ➔ Click Start session. Select the instance named Test-Interface-Endpoint. This EC2 instance resides in VPC On-Prem, simulating an on-premises host connected via VPN. The browser terminal launches with the shell prompt: sh-4.2$. 3. Generate Test Payload & Transfer via Explicit Endpoint URL Switch to the ssm-user directory:
cd ~ pwd Generate a 1GB test file named testfile2.xyz:
fallocate -l 1G testfile2.xyz ls -lh testfile2.xyz Upload the file to S3 using the AWS CLI --endpoint-url argument: aws s3 cp --endpoint-url https://bucket.<Regional-DNS-Name> testfile2.xyz s3://<your-bucket-name> [!IMPORTANT]
Replace <Regional-DNS-Name> with the exact string copied in Step 1 (e.g., vpce-0123456789abcdef0-xxxx.s3.us-east-1.vpce.amazonaws.com). Do not include wildcard asterisks *. Replace <your-bucket-name> with your actual target S3 bucket name. The --endpoint-url parameter is mandatory at this stage because the on-premises DNS has not yet been configured to conditionally resolve standard S3 domains to the interface endpoint ENI IPs. The payload transfers successfully over the StrongSwan VPN tunnel into the VPC Interface Endpoint.
4. Verify Payload in S3 Management Console Return to the Amazon S3 Console and click your bucket name. In the Objects tab, verify that testfile2.xyz is listed alongside testfile.xyz.

title: Infrastructure Observability with Grafana & Amazon CloudWatch
content:
This hands-on lab on Infrastructure Observability with Grafana & Amazon CloudWatch (Getting started with Grafana basic - Workshop 000029) was conducted on Thursday (22/10/2026) as part of Week 6. This document provides a complete, end-to-end operational guide for provisioning a Grafana monitoring host on Amazon Linux 2023, configuring secure IAM permissions, integrating Amazon CloudWatch data sources, and building customized telemetry dashboards.
🎯 Lab Objectives: Understand the hybrid monitoring architecture combining the world-leading open-source visualization suite Grafana with Amazon CloudWatch as the primary metrics repository. Master security best practices following AWS Well-Architected Framework: implement an IAM Role attached directly to the EC2 Instance Profile so Grafana retrieves ephemeral credentials automatically instead of hard-coding static Access Keys. Execute foundational network and security provisioning: verify VPC configuration, enable automatic public IPv4 addressing on the Public Subnet, and configure Security Groups allowing access to port 3000 (Grafana Web UI) and port 22 (SSH). Configure the official Grafana RPM repository, install the software packages, and run the grafana-server background daemon managed by systemd on modern Amazon Linux 2023 (AL2023). Establish a CloudWatch Data Source connection, validate API reachability (CloudWatch Metrics API and CloudWatch Logs API), design interactive Dashboards displaying CPUUtilization, and explore multi-dimensional metrics using Bar charts and Time series panels. 📊 Summary of Deployed Infrastructure & Parameters: Component / Resource Logical Name / Identifier Technical Specifications Region / AZ Operational Purpose VPC Grafana-ASG-vpc (vpc-02b25cbbec17b38ca) CIDR: 10.0.0.0/16, DNS hostnames: Enabled us-east-1 Dedicated network perimeter for observability stack Public Subnet Grafana-ASG-subnet-public1-us-east-1a (subnet-0fe0631efc71d460b) CIDR: 10.0.0.0/20, Auto-assign Public IPv4: Yes us-east-1a Public subnet for inbound web access Security Group SG-PUB-Grafana-ASG (sg-0b5bc8236a3cadcd8) Inbound: TCP 3000 (Grafana), TCP 22 (SSH), All ICMP us-east-1 Stateful firewall securing the monitoring host EC2 Instance Grafana-Server (i-082d165f34a40407f) Type: t3.micro, AMI: Amazon Linux 2023, Public IP: 44.203.10.190 us-east-1a Host instance executing the Grafana service IAM Policy GrafanaAccessPolicy CloudWatch Metrics & Logs Read-Only permissions Global Least-privilege authorization policy IAM Role GrafanaAccessRole Service: ec2.amazonaws.com, Attached: GrafanaAccessPolicy Global Instance profile granting temporary AWS credentials Grafana Server Grafana v13.3.0 Port 3000, Auth: Admin Console, Service: active (running) Host EC2 Data visualization and alerting engine Data Source CloudWatch Region: ap-southeast-1 / us-east-1, Namespace: AWS/EC2 Grafana Plugin Native connector querying telemetry APIs 🚀 Step-by-Step Implementation & Screenshot Evidence: Part 1: Network & Security Configuration Step 1: Verify Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) Setup Action: Sign in to the AWS Management Console in the us-east-1 (N. Virginia) region ➔ Open Amazon VPC ➔ Select Your VPCs. Execution: Confirm that the VPC named Grafana-ASG-vpc (vpc-02b25cbbec17b38ca) is in an Available state with DNS Hostnames and DNS Resolution fully enabled. Step 2: Enable Auto-assign Public IPv4 Address on Subnet Action: Navigate to Subnets in the left sidebar ➔ Select subnet Grafana-ASG-subnet-public1-us-east-1a (subnet-0fe0631efc71d460b). Execution: Click Actions ➔ Select Edit subnet settings ➔ Check Enable auto-assign public IPv4 address ➔ Click Save. A green confirmation banner confirms that instances launched into this subnet will receive routable public IPs automatically. Step 3: Configure Security Group Inbound Rules Action: Open Security Groups ➔ Create a new security group named SG-PUB-Grafana-ASG (sg-0b5bc8236a3cadcd8) associated with Grafana-ASG-vpc. Inbound Rules Configuration: Custom TCP - Port 3000: Permit inbound HTTP traffic to the Grafana Web UI. SSH - Port 22: Permit inbound SSH administration from authorized administrator IPs. All ICMP - IPv4: Permit ICMP diagnostic and ping connectivity checks. Part 2: EC2 Instance Provisioning & IAM Security Setup Step 4: Launch EC2 Instance Grafana-Server Action: Navigate to Amazon EC2 ➔ Click Launch instances. Instance Specification: Instance Name: Grafana-Server. OS Image (AMI): Amazon Linux 2023 (AL2023) 64-bit (x86_64). Instance Type: t3.micro (Free Tier eligible). Network Settings: Attach to Grafana-ASG-vpc, subnet Grafana-ASG-subnet-public1-us-east-1a, and assign SG-PUB-Grafana-ASG. Instance successfully initializes with ID i-082d165f34a40407f, Public IPv4 44.203.10.190, and Private IP 10.0.4.227. Step 5: Create IAM User & Issue Access Keys (Programmatic / Backup Option) Action: Navigate to IAM ➔ Select Users ➔ Click Create user with username Grafana-user. Execution: Finalize user permissions and proceed to Create access key to obtain programmatic credentials (AKIA_DEMO_SAMPLE_KEY_ID) for command-line verification and fallback access. Step 6: Create IAM Policy GrafanaAccessPolicy Action: In IAM, navigate to Policies ➔ Click Create policy. Execution: Define read-only JSON permissions targeting CloudWatch metrics and logs (cloudwatch:Describe*, cloudwatch:Get*, cloudwatch:List*, logs:DescribeLogGroups, logs:FilterLogEvents). Name the policy GrafanaAccessPolicy and create it. Step 7: Create IAM Role & Attach to EC2 Instance Profile Action: Select Roles ➔ Click Create role ➔ Choose AWS service (EC2) as the trusted entity ➔ Attach GrafanaAccessPolicy ➔ Name the role GrafanaAccessRole. Instance Profile Attachment: Return to EC2 ➔ Select Grafana-Server (i-082d165f34a40407f) ➔ Click Actions ➔ Security ➔ Modify IAM role ➔ Select GrafanaAccessRole ➔ Click Update IAM role. A green banner confirms successful attachment. Part 3: Grafana Installation & Daemon Operations on AL2023 Step 8: SSH Connection & YUM Repository Setup Action: Connect via SSH to 44.203.10.190 as ec2-user. System Update & Repository Configuration: sudo yum update -y sudo nano /etc/yum.repos.d/grafana.repo Repository Configuration Content: [grafana] name=grafana baseurl=https://rpm.grafana.com repo_gpgcheck=1 enabled=1 gpgcheck=1 gpgkey=https://rpm.grafana.com/gpg.key sslverify=1 sslcacert=/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt Step 9: Install Grafana Application Package Action: Run the automated package installer: sudo yum install grafana -y Result: The system imports Grafana Labs GPG keys (engineering@grafana.com), resolves dependencies, and installs grafana-13.3.0-1.x86_64 (installed size: ~1.3 GB). Step 10: Start grafana-server Daemon & Verify Service State Action: Reload systemd configuration, enable automatic boot startup, and launch the service: sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl enable grafana-server.service sudo systemctl start grafana-server.service sudo systemctl status grafana-server.service Verification: The daemon reports active (running) status, binding to local ports and serving HTTP requests. Step 11: Access Grafana Web UI & Update Admin Password Action: Open a web browser and navigate to http://44.203.10.190:3000. Initial Authentication: Authenticate with initial credentials admin / admin. Password Rotation: The portal immediately prompts to update default credentials to eliminate security risks (enter new password giabao2005 and submit). Part 4: CloudWatch Data Source & Dashboard Visualization Step 12: Add CloudWatch Data Source & Validate API Connectivity Action: In Grafana’s left navigation bar, choose Connections ➔ Data sources ➔ Click Add new data source ➔ Select CloudWatch. Configuration: Authentication Provider: Select AWS SDK Default (leveraging the attached EC2 instance role without static credentials). Default Region: Set to us-east-1 (or target workload region). Connection Test: Click Save & test. The green notification confirms: 1. Successfully queried the CloudWatch metrics API. 2. Successfully queried the CloudWatch logs API. Step 13: Build Time-Series Monitoring Dashboard for CPU Utilization Action: Navigate to Dashboards ➔ Click New dashboard ➔ Select Add visualization ➔ Choose cloudwatch. Query Builder Parameters: Namespace: AWS/EC2. Metric name: CPUUtilization. Statistic: Average. Dimensions: Filter by InstanceId = i-082d165f34a40407f. Result: A live Time-Series graph updates in real time displaying host CPU workload patterns. Step 14: Advanced Metric Exploration with Explore Tool Action: In the main menu, click Explore ➔ Select cloudwatch data source. Ad-hoc Query: Target region: ap-southeast-1. Metric: CPUUtilization, Dimension: InstanceId = i-0ba9a1a9ccab2d73f. Switch visualization mode to Bars to highlight workload spikes with distinct clarity. 💡 Lessons Learned & Troubleshooting Bank: Below are 5 practical troubleshooting scenarios encountered during Grafana and CloudWatch deployment, accompanied by verified root causes and solutions:
1. Inability to Access Grafana Web UI on Port 3000 (Connection Timed Out) Root Cause: The EC2 Security Group lacked an Inbound rule permitting TCP traffic on port 3000 from client IP ranges, or the instance was provisioned in an isolated subnet lacking an Internet Gateway route. Remediation: Inspect SG-PUB-Grafana-ASG Inbound rules and verify that Custom TCP on port 3000 is open. Confirm the subnet route table points 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway (igw-xxxx). 2. CloudWatch Data Source Authorization Error (AccessDeniedException / HTTP 403) Root Cause: The IAM Role attached to the EC2 instance lacked permissions required to invoke CloudWatch or CloudWatch Logs metric queries. Remediation: Ensure GrafanaAccessPolicy includes complete read-only actions: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowGrafanaCloudWatchAccess", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "cloudwatch:DescribeAlarmsForMetric", "cloudwatch:DescribeAlarmHistory", "cloudwatch:DescribeAlarms", "cloudwatch:ListMetrics", "cloudwatch:GetMetricStatistics", "cloudwatch:GetMetricData", "logs:DescribeLogGroups", "logs:GetLogGroupFields", "logs:StartQuery", "logs:StopQuery", "logs:GetQueryResults", "logs:GetLogEvents", "ec2:DescribeTags", "ec2:DescribeInstances", "ec2:DescribeRegions" ], "Resource": "*" } ] } 3. Best Practice: EC2 IAM Instance Profile vs Static Access Keys Analysis: Hard-coding IAM user Access Key ID and Secret Access Key into web application configuration violates the principle of least privilege and introduces credential exposure risks. Architectural Guidance: Always use AWS SDK Default authentication on AWS-hosted Grafana instances. Grafana retrieves rotating, temporary tokens via the Instance Metadata Service (IMDSv2) automatically. 4. grafana-server Service Fails to Start Automatically on Instance Reboot Root Cause: Administrator manually executed systemctl start grafana-server without enabling the systemd service unit. Remediation: Always run sudo systemctl enable grafana-server. Confirm configuration via systemctl is-enabled grafana-server (expected output: enabled). 5. Clean-Up Lifecycle to Prevent Cloud Charges (Resource Cleanup) Decommissioning Steps: Terminate the EC2 host Grafana-Server (i-082d165f34a40407f). Detach and delete GrafanaAccessRole and GrafanaAccessPolicy. Delete security group SG-PUB-Grafana-ASG. Delete the custom VPC Grafana-ASG-vpc to release associated subnets and Internet Gateway resources.

title: Deploy Amazon ElastiCache - Redis
content:
The Amazon ElastiCache - Redis workshop was conducted on Wednesday (10/14/2026) as part of Week 5. This document presents a comprehensive technical walkthrough: AWS Console configurations, infrastructure specifications, RBAC security hardening with Users and User Groups, programmatic automation with AWS CLI & Python Boto3 SDK, as well as hands-on troubleshooting of real-world operational challenges. 🔗 Reference Documentation: Amazon ElastiCache - Redis
🎯 Lab Objectives: Design and provision an isolated VPC network topology with 3 Subnets distributed across 3 Availability Zones (us-east-1a, us-east-1b, us-east-1c) and configure an ElastiCache Subnet Group to satisfy Multi-AZ high availability and data sharding requirements. Configure Security Group firewall policies permitting inbound traffic on TCP port 6379 (Redis) and TCP port 22 (SSH). Provision an intermediate Amazon EC2 Client (redis-client) within the same VPC to interface with the private, isolated cache clusters. Deploy and manage Redis clusters across both fundamental architectures: Cluster Mode Disabled: 1 Shard, 1 Primary node, and 2 Replica nodes with automated failover (Auto-failover). Cluster Mode Enabled: Multi-shard distributed architecture (3 Shards, 9 Nodes) enabling horizontal scaling and hash slot partitioning. Fully automate Redis cluster provisioning utilizing the AWS CLI and the Python Boto3 SDK. Implement enterprise-grade security controls: Transit Encryption (TLS) paired with Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) using custom Users and User Groups. Develop Python client scripts to interact with Redis: cluster connectivity verification, string storage (Strings) with Time-to-Live (TTL), hash map data structures (Hash), and real-time asynchronous message streaming (Pub/Sub). Resolve 12 critical technical challenges (Route Table Blackholes, missing package managers, deprecated third-party libraries, WRONGTYPE schema collisions, and User Group dependency errors). 📊 Provisioned Resource Specifications: Resource Name / Identifier Technical Configuration & Specs Region / AZ Notes VPC vpc-0fc9d5490a843944e CIDR: 10.0.0.0/16, attached Internet Gateway my-igw us-east-1 Isolated network environment for ElastiCache Subnet Group subnet-group 3 subnets spanning 3 distinct Availability Zones us-east-1a, 1b, 1c Satisfies Multi-AZ & Sharding topology constraints Security Group sg-06c03603fe1cca808 Inbound: Port 22 (SSH), Port 6379 (Redis) us-east-1 Firewall protecting EC2 and ElastiCache EC2 Redis Client redis-client ID: i-02673f346989f7c23, AL2023, Python 3 + redis v8.1.0 us-east-1a Bastion client accessed via EC2 Instance Connect Cluster 1 (Console) my-cluster-disable Mode: Disabled, cache.r6g.large, 1 Shard, 3 Nodes, Multi-AZ us-east-1 Primary Endpoint: my-cluster-disable.1vblox.ng.0001.use1...:6379 Cluster 2 (Console) my-cluster-enable Mode: Enabled, cache.r6g.large, 3 Shards, 9 Nodes, Multi-AZ us-east-1 Config Endpoint: my-cluster-enable.1vblox.clustercfg.use1...:6379 Cluster 3 (SDK) redis-disabled-sdk Mode: Disabled, cache.t4g.micro, Engine 6.0, 2 Nodes us-east-1 Automated provisioning via Boto3 script Cluster 4 (SDK) redis-enabled-sdk Mode: Enabled, cache.t4g.micro, 2 Shards, 4 Nodes us-east-1 Automated provisioning via Boto3 script Cluster 5 (SDK + RBAC) redis-rbac-sdk Mode: Disabled, Transit Encryption: True, UserGroup: mygroup us-east-1 Primary Endpoint: master.redis-rbac-sdk.1vblox.use1...:6379 Cluster 6 (SDK + RBAC) redis-enabled-rbac-sdk Mode: Enabled, 2 Shards, TLS Encryption: True, UserGroup: mygroup us-east-1 Sharded cluster protected by TLS and RBAC RBAC User Group mygroup, mygroup2 User Groups governing authenticated client access Global / Regional Bound to TLS-enabled Redis clusters RBAC Users myuser, default Password: MyStrongPasswordWithNumbers123, Access: on ~* +@all Global / Regional Assigned to User Groups mygroup and mygroup2 📋 Section 1: Environment Preparation & Identity Management (Prerequisites) Step 1: Create IAM User for ElastiCache Administration Action: Navigate to the AWS Management Console ➔ Access IAM ➔ Select Users in the left navigation pane ➔ Click Create user. Configuration: User name: ElastiCache Permissions options: Select Attach policies directly ➔ Attach AmazonElastiCacheFullAccess and AdministratorAccess to facilitate automated administration. Objective: Establish a dedicated programmatic identity for ElastiCache operations via AWS CLI and Python SDK. Step 2: Install and Verify AWS CLI v2 Action: Open Windows Command Prompt (cmd.exe). Command: msiexec.exe /i https://awscli.amazonaws.com/AWSCLIV2.msi aws --version Output: AWS CLI v2 successfully installed: aws-cli/2.38.1 Python/3.14.6 Windows/11 exe/AMD64. Step 3: Configure AWS CLI Credentials Action: Configure the local CLI profile with the newly provisioned IAM User credentials. Command: aws configure Parameters: AWS Access Key ID: AKIA_DEMO_SAMPLE_KEY_ID AWS Secret Access Key: DEMO_SECRET_KEY_SAMPLE_TEST_12345 Default region name: us-east-1 (or ap-southeast-1) Default output format: json 📋 Section 2: VPC Networking & Web Console Redis Provisioning Step 4: Create Multi-AZ ElastiCache Subnet Group Action: In the AWS Console ➔ Search for Amazon ElastiCache ➔ Select Subnet groups in the left pane ➔ Click Create subnet group. Parameters: Name: subnet-group Description: test ElastiCache VPC ID: Select VPC vpc-0fc9d5490a843944e Subnets: Select subnets across at least 2 distinct Availability Zones (select all 3 subnets in us-east-1a, us-east-1b, us-east-1c). Action: Click Create to initialize the Subnet Group. 💡 Troubleshooting Note for Step 4 (Availability Zone Requirements): ElastiCache clusters configured with Multi-AZ or Cluster Mode Enabled require nodes to be distributed across at least two distinct Availability Zones. Associating subnets from only one AZ will cause AWS to disable cluster creation or return the error Each Node Group needs to have at least two distinct Availability Zones. Always ensure subnets from at least 2 to 3 distinct AZs are added to the subnet-group.
Step 5: Verify Subnet Group Configuration via AWS CLI Action: Query the newly provisioned subnet group from the command line. Command: aws elasticache describe-cache-subnet-groups --cache-subnet-group-name subnet-group --region us-east-1 Output: Returns a JSON payload showing VpcId, SubnetIdentifier list (subnet-0fdbddde41a5c456d), SubnetAvailabilityZone (us-east-1a), and the associated ARN. Step 6: Provision Cluster Mode Disabled Redis Cluster on Web Console Action: In the ElastiCache Console ➔ Select Redis OSS caches ➔ Click Create Redis OSS cache. Configuration: Cluster name: my-cluster-disable Description: create cluster Node type: cache.r6g.large Engine version: 6.2.6 Cluster mode: Disabled Shards: 1 Number of nodes: 3 (1 Primary + 2 Replicas) Multi-AZ: Enabled Auto-failover: Enabled Subnet group: Select subnet-group Output: Cluster enters Available status. Retrieve the Primary endpoint (my-cluster-disable.1vblox.ng.0001.use1.cache.amazonaws.com:6379) and Reader endpoint (my-cluster-disable-ro.1vblox.ng.0001.use1.cache.amazonaws.com:6379). Step 7: Provision Cluster Mode Enabled Redis Cluster on Web Console Action: In Redis OSS caches ➔ Click Create Redis OSS cache. Configuration: Cluster name: my-cluster-enable Description: create cluster enable Node type: cache.r6g.large Engine version: 6.2.6 Cluster mode: Enabled Shards: 3 Replicas per shard: 2 (Total 9 nodes) Multi-AZ: Enabled Auto-failover: Enabled Subnet group: Select subnet-group Output: Successfully provisioned cluster providing a unified Configuration endpoint: my-cluster-enable.1vblox.clustercfg.use1.cache.amazonaws.com:6379. Step 8: Configure Security Group Rules for Redis and EC2 Action: Navigate to VPC Console ➔ Security Groups ➔ Select default security group (sg-06c03603fe1cca808) ➔ Click Edit inbound rules. Inbound Rules: Rule 1 (Redis): Type: Custom TCP, Port range: 6379, Source: sg-06c03603fe1cca808 (or VPC CIDR 10.0.0.0/16) to allow inter-VPC cache communication. Rule 2 (SSH): Type: SSH, Port range: 22, Source: 0.0.0.0/0 to enable EC2 Instance Connect. Action: Click Save rules. 💡 Troubleshooting Note for Step 8 (Route Table Blackhole Mitigation): Network testing revealed that the EC2 client could not reach external package repositories and connection attempts timed out. Inspecting the VPC Route Table showed that route 0.0.0.0/0 targeted a previously detached/deleted Internet Gateway, leaving the routing state in a Blackhole. To resolve this, a new Internet Gateway named my-igw was created and attached to VPC vpc-0fc9d5490a843944e. The blackhole route was purged and replaced with 0.0.0.0/0 -> my-igw.
Step 9: Inspect Nodes and Retrieve Primary Endpoint Action: Open my-cluster-disable ➔ Navigate to the Nodes tab. Observation: Three nodes are operational: my-cluster-disable-001 (Role: primary), 002 (Role: replica), and 003 (Role: replica). Copy the Primary endpoint for write operations. Step 10: Inspect Shards and Distributed Endpoints for Cluster Mode Enabled Action: Open my-cluster-enable ➔ Switch to the Shards and nodes tab. Observation: Review the distribution across 3 Shards and 9 constituent nodes (my-cluster-enable-0001-001, 002, 003) along with their respective individual node endpoints and assigned hash slot allocations. Step 11: Inspect Cache Cluster Node via AWS CLI Action: Open Command Prompt to query individual node metadata. Command: aws elasticache describe-cache-clusters --cache-cluster-id my-cluster-enable-0001-001 --show-cache-node-info --region us-east-1 Output: Validates engine version 6.2.6, available status, maintenance schedules, endpoints, and parameter group sync state. Step 12: Query Replication Group Metadata via AWS CLI Action: Validate the distributed cluster slot partitions across the replication group. Command: aws elasticache describe-replication-groups --replication-group-id my-cluster-enable --region us-east-1 Output: Confirms NodeGroups with Slots: "0-5461", validating that the cluster is healthy and primed for distributed operations. 📋 Section 3: Programmatic Automation via Python Boto3 SDK & RBAC Administration Step 13: Provision Cluster Mode Disabled Cluster via SDK (CreateClusterModeDisabledCluster.py) Action: In Windows PowerShell, switch to the project root and trigger automated provisioning: Command: cd d:\AWS\template_AWS\fcj-workshop-template-main python CreateClusterModeDisabledCluster.py Output: Boto3 invokes the create_replication_group API, creating cluster redis-disabled-sdk with NumCacheClusters=2, CacheNodeType='cache.t4g.micro', initial status creating, and HTTP response code 200. Step 14: ⚠️ Critical Incident: RBAC Cluster Creation Failure When User Group (testusergroup / mygroup) Does Not Exist Action: Attempt to provision an encrypted Redis cluster bound to an RBAC User Group: python ClusterModeDisabledWithRBAC.py Observed Error Stack: The execution halts immediately with a fatal Boto3 client exception: Traceback (most recent call last): File "D:\AWS\template_AWS\fcj-workshop-template-main\ClusterModeDisabledWithRBAC.py", line 62, in <module> response = create_cluster_mode_disabled_rbac(...) File "D:\AWS\template_AWS\fcj-workshop-template-main\ClusterModeDisabledWithRBAC.py", line 56, in create_cluster_mode_disabled_rbac response = client.create_replication_group(**params) botocore.errorfactory.UserGroupNotFoundFault: An error occurred (UserGroupNotFound) when calling the CreateReplicationGroup operation: User group mygroup not found. Root Cause Analysis: The script specifies UserGroupIds=['mygroup'] (or testusergroup in standard lab templates). However, no User Group with this ID exists on the ElastiCache service at this point! During CreateReplicationGroup validation, AWS confirms the existence of all specified UserGroupIds. Because mygroup has not yet been provisioned, the API rejects the request and throws UserGroupNotFoundFault. Step 15: Provision Cluster Mode Enabled Cluster via SDK (ClusterModeEnabled.py) Action: In parallel, provision an automated multi-shard cluster: python ClusterModeEnabled.py Output: Successfully initializes cluster redis-enabled-sdk featuring 2 Shards and 4 Nodes with ClusterEnabled: True and HTTP response code 200. Step 16: Re-confirming User Group Prerequisite Dependency Observation: Repeating execution of ClusterModeDisabledWithRBAC.py before creating the User Group confirms the identical UserGroupNotFoundFault exception, validating that User Groups are a strict prerequisite for RBAC-secured clusters. Step 17: ✅ Remediation: Provision RBAC Users and User Groups via UserAndUserGroups.py Resolution Strategy: Execute the Python script UserAndUserGroups.py to provision the full RBAC identity hierarchy: Create application user: mygroup-myuser (UserName: myuser) with password MyStrongPasswordWithNumbers123 and access string on ~* +@all (granting full privileges across all keys and command categories). Create mandatory default user: mygroup-default (UserName: default), fulfilling the ElastiCache RBAC requirement that every group contains a default administrative user. Create User Group mygroup (or testusergroup): Bind mygroup-myuser and mygroup-default into the group. Concurrently provision a standby group mygroup2 (mygroup2-myuser2 and mygroup2-default). Command: python UserAndUserGroups.py Output: All Users and User Groups provisioned successfully with valid ARNs: arn:aws:elasticache:us-east-1:887086382708:user:mygroup-myuser arn:aws:elasticache:us-east-1:887086382708:user:mygroup-default arn:aws:elasticache:us-east-1:887086382708:usergroup:mygroup Step 18: 🎉 Successful Execution: Re-running RBAC Cluster Creation After User Group Exists! Action: Re-execute the RBAC cluster provisioning script now that mygroup exists: python ClusterModeDisabledWithRBAC.py Output: The UserGroupNotFoundFault error is completely eliminated! The request succeeds with HTTP status 200. Cluster redis-rbac-sdk transitions to creating with TransitEncryptionEnabled: True and successfully binds to UserGroupIds: ['mygroup']. Step 19: Provision Sharded Cluster with TLS and RBAC Action: Execute ClusterModeEnabledWithRBAC.py to launch a multi-shard cluster protected by TLS Transit Encryption and User Group mygroup. Command: python ClusterModeEnabledWithRBAC.py Output: Cluster redis-enabled-rbac-sdk initializes with 2 Shards, TransitEncryptionEnabled: True, UserGroupIds: ['mygroup'], and ClusterMode: 'enabled'. 📋 Section 4: EC2 Client Environment & Programmatic Data Operations Step 20: Resolve Missing pip3 and Install redis Library on EC2 Client Action: Open AWS Console ➔ Select instance redis-client (i-02673f346989f7c23) ➔ Connect via EC2 Instance Connect. Observed Issue: Running pip3 install redis returns: -bash: pip3: command not found Resolution: Install python3-pip via Amazon Linux package repositories, then install the Python redis driver: sudo dnf install -y python3-pip && pip3 install redis Output: Library redis-7.0.1 installed successfully. Step 21: Verify TLS Encrypted Redis Connection with RBAC Credentials Action: Test authenticated TLS connectivity to redis-rbac-sdk using myuser credentials: Command: python3 -c " from redis import Redis redis = Redis( host='master.redis-rbac-sdk.1vblox.use1.cache.amazonaws.com', port=6379, decode_responses=True, ssl=True, username='myuser', password='MyStrongPasswordWithNumbers123' ) if redis.ping(): print('>>> CONNECTED TO REDIS SUCCESSFULLY! <<<') " Output: Confirms connection: >>> CONNECTED TO REDIS SUCCESSFULLY! <<<. 💡 Critical Network Security Architecture: Amazon ElastiCache clusters reside strictly within VPC Private Subnets, have no Public IPs, and lack direct Internet routing. Any attempt to reach the cache from a local workstation will trigger a Connection Timed Out. All administrative and data access must originate from an EC2 client residing within the same VPC.
Step 22: Connect to Cluster Mode Enabled Cluster (ConnectClusterModeEnabled.py) Action: Connect to sharded cluster my-cluster-enable using the modern official SDK syntax: Command: cat << 'EOF' > ConnectClusterModeEnabled.py from redis.cluster import RedisCluster import logging logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) # Target configuration endpoint of my-cluster-enable redis = RedisCluster( host="my-cluster-enable.1vblox.clustercfg.use1.cache.amazonaws.com", port=6379, decode_responses=True ) if redis.ping(): logging.info("Connected to Redis") EOF python3 ConnectClusterModeEnabled.py Output: Emits: INFO:root:Connected to Redis. 💡 Troubleshooting Note for Step 22 (Library Deprecation): Original lab instructions recommend from rediscluster import RedisCluster. That third-party package (redis-py-cluster) is obsolete and unmaintained. Cluster capabilities are now natively bundled inside the primary redis library. Use from redis.cluster import RedisCluster and replace placeholder endpoints (xxx.yyy...) with the actual cluster Configuration Endpoint.
Step 23: String Operations and Time-to-Live Expiration (SetAndGetStrings.py) Action: Execute a script storing key mykey with a 60-second TTL (ex=60), sleep for 5 seconds, and verify TTL countdown. Command: python3 SetAndGetStrings.py Output: Displays remaining TTL: 2026-10-19 14:45:28,612: Key mykey was set at Mon Oct 19 14:45:23 2026 and has 55 seconds until expired Step 24: Hash Map Data Structures (SetAndGetHash.py) Action: Store a Hash object containing datetime and epochtime fields, including a preemptive key deletion to avoid data type collisions. Command: python3 SetAndGetHash.py Output: 2026-10-19 14:49:02,703: Key mykey was set at {'datetime': 'Mon Oct 19 14:48:57 2026', 'epochtime': '1792421337.696463'} and has 55 seconds until expired 💡 Troubleshooting Note for Step 24 (WRONGTYPE Data Collision): Step 23 stored key mykey as a String. In Step 24, attempting an immediate hset against mykey before its 60-second TTL expires will trigger WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value. Prepend redis.delete(keyName) to clear existing data before writing the Hash.
Step 25: Real-Time Asynchronous Message Streaming with Pub/Sub (PubAndSub.py) Action: Launch an asynchronous subscriber thread via run_in_thread listening on channel mychannel, while the main loop publishes timestamped payloads. Command: python3 PubAndSub.py Output: Subscriber stream processes messages in sub-millisecond intervals: INFO:root:{'type': 'message', 'pattern': None, 'channel': 'mychannel', 'data': 'My message'} INFO:root:{'type': 'message', 'pattern': None, 'channel': 'mychannel', 'data': 'Mon Oct 19 15:03:07 2026'} INFO:root:{'type': 'message', 'pattern': None, 'channel': 'mychannel', 'data': 'Mon Oct 19 15:03:08 2026'} Step 26: Pub/Sub Stream Verification and Graceful Termination Observation: The real-time messaging pipeline maintains sub-millisecond throughput. Wrapping the execution in try...except KeyboardInterrupt ensures clean detachment upon pressing Ctrl + C. 🔍 Summary of 12 Technical Challenges & Production Resolutions: Route Table Blackhole Causing Complete Network Disconnection: Symptom: EC2 Instance Connect failed and external package installations timed out. Root Cause: Default route 0.0.0.0/0 referenced a detached/deleted Internet Gateway. Resolution: Attached new gateway my-igw and re-pointed 0.0.0.0/0 -> my-igw. Missing pip3 Package Manager (-bash: pip3: command not found): Symptom: Package installation aborted on Amazon Linux 2023. Root Cause: Minimalist OS footprint omits pip by default. Resolution: Executed sudo dnf install -y python3-pip. Missing Redis Client Driver (ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'redis'): Symptom: Script execution failed due to missing Redis driver. Root Cause: Environment lacked the redis-py library. Resolution: Executed pip3 install redis. Deprecated rediscluster Third-Party Library: Symptom: from rediscluster import RedisCluster failed. Root Cause: Legacy package has been deprecated and merged into official redis. Resolution: Updated code to from redis.cluster import RedisCluster. Template Placeholder Endpoints (xxx.yyy...): Symptom: Failed hostname resolution. Root Cause: Sample documentation used dummy placeholder strings. Resolution: Replaced with the active Configuration Endpoint from the console. Missing Redis Connection Initialization in Sample Code: Symptom: NameError: name 'redis' is not defined. Root Cause: Workshop assumed an active interactive shell session where the client had already been declared. Resolution: Prepended explicit RedisCluster(...) connection instantiation in both scripts. Data Structure Collision (WRONGTYPE): Symptom: WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value. Root Cause: Key mykey retained its String datatype during its active 60-second TTL window. Resolution: Added redis.delete(keyName) prior to invoking hset. Pub/Sub Import Omission and Terminal Hang: Symptom: NameError: name 'Redis' is not defined and unstoppable infinite loop. Root Cause: Missing from redis import Redis import and absence of signal handling. Resolution: Added import and encapsulated the loop inside try...except KeyboardInterrupt. Inability to Connect from Local Workstation (Connection Timed Out): Symptom: Local Python scripts timed out. Root Cause: ElastiCache resides in private subnets with no public Internet ingress. Resolution: Provisioned an in-VPC EC2 client and opened port 6379 in the security group. Subnet Group Multi-AZ Constraint Failures: Symptom: Each Node Group needs to have at least two distinct Availability Zones. Root Cause: Multi-AZ and Sharded clusters mandate nodes across at least two distinct AZs. Resolution: Configured subnet-group with 3 subnets spanning us-east-1a, us-east-1b, and us-east-1c. Critical Failure When Provisioning RBAC Clusters Without User Group (UserGroupNotFoundFault): Symptom: ClusterModeDisabledWithRBAC.py threw UserGroupNotFoundFault: User group mygroup not found. Root Cause: The target UserGroupIds=['mygroup'] (or testusergroup) did not yet exist in ElastiCache. Resolution: Executed UserAndUserGroups.py to provision myuser, the mandatory default user, and group mygroup. Re-executing cluster creation succeeded with HTTP 200. Python Function Signature Syntax Error in Sample Code: Symptom: SyntaxError: non-default argument follows default argument. Root Cause: Parameter without default value placed after parameters with default values. Resolution: Assigned default value CacheSubnetGroupName=None to standardize the signature.

title: Monitoring with Amazon CloudWatch
content:
The Monitoring with Amazon CloudWatch hands-on lab was conducted on Thursday (08/10/2026) during Week 4. This page provides a comprehensive step-by-step implementation guide featuring precise configuration parameters, Logs Insights query syntax, Math Expressions, troubleshooting resolutions, and all 33 verification screenshots. 🔗 Lab Reference Material: Monitoring with Amazon CloudWatch
🎯 Lab Objectives: Master the centralized monitoring and observability capabilities of Amazon CloudWatch on AWS. Visualize and analyze real-time performance metrics (CloudWatch Metrics) across cloud infrastructure. Utilize Search Expressions and Math Expressions to dynamically discover, aggregate, and normalize telemetry data. Configure Dynamic Labels for context-aware and automated chart legends. Ingest and analyze system logs (CloudWatch Logs) using the interactive query language CloudWatch Logs Insights. Establish Metric Filters to extract actionable quantitative metrics from unstructured application log streams. Configure CloudWatch Alarms integrated with Amazon SNS to automate proactive incident alerting. 📊 Provisioned Resource Specifications: Resource Name / Identifier Configuration & Detailed Specs Region / Status Notes EC2 Instance Monitored Web-Server-Lab Amazon Linux 2023, CloudWatch Agent installed ap-southeast-1 Telemetry & log collection Metric Monitored CPUUtilization, DiskReadBytes Namespace: AWS/EC2, Period: 1 minute Real-time monitoring Graphical performance telemetry Search Expression SEARCH(' {AWS/EC2,InstanceId} MetricName="CPUUtilization" ', 'Average', 300) Automated metric query across all fleet instances Dynamic Dashboard Self-updating on new instance launch Math Expression m1 * 100 / MAX(m1) Normalizes CPU utilization proportionally Math plot expression Mathematical data modeling Log Group /aws/ec2/system-logs Retention: 7 days Ingestion: Active OS and web server access logs Metric Filter HTTP404ErrorCount Pattern: [ip, user, username, timestamp, request, status_code = 404, size] Namespace: Custom/Web Counts HTTP 404 errors from access logs CloudWatch Alarm High-CPU-Utilization-Alarm Static threshold: CPU > 70% across 2 periods Status: OK / ALARM Dispatches automated SNS email alerts 🚀 Step-by-Step Implementation & Screenshot Gallery: Step 1: Environment Setup & CloudWatch Agent Installation on EC2 Action / Navigation: Launch EC2 instance Web-Server-Lab, attach IAM Role with policy CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy ➔ Connect via SSH and install the agent package. Commands Executed: # Install CloudWatch Agent package sudo yum install -y amazon-cloudwatch-agent # Start CloudWatch Agent daemon with configuration file sudo /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl \ -a fetch-config -m ec2 -s -c file:/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Troubleshooting at Step 1:
If the EC2 instance lacks the CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy IAM Role, log writes in /var/log/amazon/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.log will fail with an AccessDeniedException. Always ensure IAM Role assignment prior to starting the agent service.
Step 2: Explore CloudWatch All Metrics Dashboard Action / Navigation: In the CloudWatch Console ➔ Sidebar select Metrics ➔ All metrics. Purpose: Inspect default namespaces populated automatically by AWS (e.g., AWS/EC2, AWS/EBS, AWS/ApplicationELB). Step 3: Select Per-Instance EC2 Telemetry Metrics Action / Navigation: Under All metrics, navigate to EC2 ➔ Click Per-Instance Metrics. Configuration: Locate the target Instance ID and check CPUUtilization, NetworkIn, and DiskReadBytes. Step 4: Customize Metric Visualization (Graphed Metrics) Action / Navigation: Switch to the Graphed metrics tab. Configuration: Toggle line visibility, assign unique colors, and associate series with left or right Y-axes. Step 5: Adjust Aggregation Period and Statistics Action / Navigation: Under the Statistic column, change to Average. Under Period, select 1 Minute for high-resolution sampling. Step 6: Render High-Fidelity Real-Time CPU Graph Action / Navigation: Adjust the time-window selector to 1h (last 1 hour). Observation: The plot details granular 1-minute CPU variations in real time. Step 7: Define Dynamic Search Expression Query Action / Navigation: In Graphed metrics, click Add math ➔ Search expression. Search Expression Syntax: SEARCH(' {AWS/EC2,InstanceId} MetricName="CPUUtilization" ', 'Average', 300) Purpose: Dynamically discovers and plots CPU utilization across all current and future EC2 instances without manual selection. 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Troubleshooting at Step 7:
Search Expression syntax is sensitive to spacing and curly brace syntax {} for dimensions. Ensure metric and dimension names match exact casing (MetricName="CPUUtilization").
Step 8: Multi-Instance Telemetry Visualization via Search Expression Action / Navigation: Click Apply. Observation: The graph renders discrete lines for all active instances in the region automatically. Step 9: Audit Matched Metric Streams Action / Navigation: Expand the query results below the chart. Observation: All matching instance telemetry streams are indexed with associated Instance IDs. Step 10: Apply Mathematical Expressions to Metric Series Action / Navigation: Click Add math ➔ Start with empty expression. Formula Applied: (m1 / 100) * 100 Purpose: Normalizes data scales or computes ratios across distinct network interfaces. Step 11: Configure Dynamic Labels from Resource Properties Action / Navigation: In the Label column, enter the property interpolation variable. Expression Syntax: ${PROP('Dim.InstanceId')} - CPU Load Purpose: Replaces cryptic metric identifiers with human-readable instance IDs in the chart legend. Step 12: Validate Formatted Dashboard Graph Action / Navigation: Review the finalized graph. Observation: The legend renders dynamic contextual labels, ready to pin to an executive dashboard. Step 13: Access CloudWatch Logs Groups Console Action / Navigation: In the sidebar, select Logs ➔ Log groups. Selection: Open the /aws/ec2/system-logs log group ingested by the CloudWatch Agent. Step 14: Inspect Per-Instance Log Streams Action / Navigation: Inside /aws/ec2/system-logs, select the Log streams tab. Observation: Dedicated streams are partitioned per EC2 Instance ID. Step 15: Review Raw System Log Event Records Action / Navigation: Click a specific log stream to review raw event rows. Observation: Operating system events, boot logs, and application outputs are preserved with UTC/Local timestamps. Step 16: Launch CloudWatch Logs Insights Query Editor Action / Navigation: Sidebar select Logs ➔ Logs Insights. Configuration: In Select log group(s), choose /aws/ec2/system-logs. Step 17: Execute Query to Filter Error Messages Action / Navigation: Input the error extraction query. Query Syntax: fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /(?i)(error|exception|fail)/ | sort @timestamp desc | limit 20 Next Action: Click Run query. Step 18: Analyze Logs Insights Tabular Results Action / Navigation: Examine the tabular records returned by the query engine. Observation: Matching error events are isolated with timestamp and message payloads. Step 19: Visualize Error Occurrence Frequency Over Time Action / Navigation: Switch to the Visualization tab ➔ Select Line chart. Observation: Error volume over time displays spike frequencies clearly. Step 20: Aggregate Distribution by HTTP Status Code Action / Navigation: Execute an aggregation query across HTTP response codes. Query Syntax: stats count(*) by status_code Result: Breaks down requests into 200 (OK), 404 (Not Found), and 500 (Server Error) buckets. Step 21: Parse Custom Log Fields (Pattern Extraction) Action / Navigation: Use the parse command to extract IP, method, and URI from raw web logs. Query Syntax: parse @message "* * [*] \"* * *\" * *" as client_ip, user, timestamp, method, uri, protocol, status, bytes | display client_ip, method, uri, status Step 22: Query Top Ingress Client IP Addresses Action / Navigation: Extract and sort the highest-frequency requester IP addresses. Query Syntax: stats count(*) as request_count by client_ip | sort request_count desc | limit 10 Step 23: Save Optimized Query to Library Action / Navigation: Click Save in the top right ➔ Name the query Top-Error-Analysis. Step 24: Re-load Query from Saved Queries Pane Action / Navigation: Select the Queries tab to reload and execute previously curated queries. Step 25: Inspect Event Record Metadata and Details Action / Navigation: Expand an event record row using the dropdown arrow to inspect JSON fields. Step 26: Optimize Query Time-Range Scan Window Action / Navigation: Adjust the time-window selector (e.g., 15m, 1h) to reduce ingested bytes scanned and enhance execution speed. Step 27: Create Metric Filter from Log Group Action / Navigation: In Log groups ➔ Select /aws/ec2/system-logs ➔ Click Metric filters tab ➔ Click Create metric filter. Step 28: Define HTTP 404 Filter Pattern Action / Navigation: Configure the pattern matching syntax. Filter Pattern Syntax: [ip, user, username, timestamp, request, status_code = 404, size] 💡 Difficulties Encountered & Troubleshooting at Step 28:
Space-delimited patterns [field1, field2, ...] require standard Apache/Nginx combined log formatting. For JSON logs, use JSON path filters { $.status_code = 404 }. Always test patterns before saving.
Step 29: Test Filter Pattern Against Sample Logs Action / Navigation: Select sample log streams and click Test pattern. Observation: Test results verify matching lines and validate tokenized fields. Step 30: Assign Metric Name, Value, and Custom Namespace Action / Navigation: Click Next to proceed to metric naming. Configuration Parameters: Metric namespace: Custom/Web Metric name: HTTP404ErrorCount Metric value: 1 Default value: 0 Step 31: Finalize Metric Filter Provisioning Action / Navigation: Click Create metric filter. Observation: The filter is active and immediately populates the metric series HTTP404ErrorCount under All Metrics. Step 32: Configure CloudWatch Alarm on CPU Threshold (> 70%) Action / Navigation: In the sidebar, select Alarms ➔ Click Create alarm ➔ Select CPUUtilization for Web-Server-Lab. title: Accessing S3 from On-Premises via Interface Endpoint
content:
Hybrid Cloud Architecture Overview When workloads hosted inside on-premises corporate datacenters require low-latency, private connectivity to Amazon S3, Gateway VPC Endpoints cannot serve this requirement because gateway endpoints are restricted to the local VPC route table.
AWS solves this hybrid connectivity challenge via Interface VPC Endpoints powered by AWS PrivateLink:
Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs): Allocates private IP addresses from your VPC subnets (10.0.x.x) to act as entry points for S3 traffic. Hybrid Network Extension: Because ENIs carry private routable IP addresses, on-premises systems can reach them over an AWS Site-to-Site VPN tunnel or AWS Direct Connect dedicated circuit. Seamless DNS Integration: Leverages Amazon Route 53 Resolver conditional forwarding to resolve standard S3 endpoints (s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com) directly to the private interface endpoint IPs. Execution Roadmap: 5.4.1 Infrastructure Preparation & VPN Routing — Configure StrongSwan VPN routing table target and deploy Route 53 Resolver endpoints. 5.4.2 Create S3 Interface Endpoint — Provision multi-AZ interface endpoints with dedicated security groups. 5.4.3 Test Direct Connectivity via Endpoint URL — Execute AWS CLI transfer commands with the --endpoint-url flag from simulated on-premises hosts. 5.4.4 Configure Route 53 Conditional DNS Forwarding — Configure Private Hosted Zone alias records and resolver rules for transparent DNS resolution.

title: Simulating On-Premises DNS via Route 53 Resolver
content:
Hybrid DNS Architecture Objectives AWS PrivateLink Interface Endpoints allocate static private IP addresses (ENIs) across selected Availability Zones. Requiring application workloads to pass an explicit --endpoint-url argument is cumbersome and lacks automated failover if an ENI becomes unreachable.
The enterprise architecture solution pairs Amazon Route 53 Private Hosted Zones with Route 53 Resolver Conditional Forwarding Rules:
On-Premises DNS Server: Forwards queries for s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com across the VPN to a Route 53 Inbound Resolver Endpoint in the VPC. Route 53 Private Hosted Zone: Resolves the query to the private IP addresses of the S3 Interface Endpoint. On-premises applications can use default AWS CLI commands and SDK clients without specifying custom --endpoint-url parameters. 1. Create DNS Alias Records in Private Hosted Zone Open the Route 53 Hosted Zones Console. Select the Private Hosted Zone named s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com (provisioned earlier via CloudFormation). Create the Apex Alias Record: Click Create record. Record name: Leave blank (targets the zone apex s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com). Record type: A - Routes traffic to an IPv4 address and some AWS resources. Alias toggle: Set to Enabled. Route traffic to: Select Alias to VPC Endpoint. Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1]. Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS copied in step 5.4.3. Create the Wildcard Alias Record: Click Add another record. Record name: Enter * (enables virtual-hosted-style bucket requests: *.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com). Record type: A Alias toggle: Enabled ➔ Alias to VPC Endpoint ➔ Region us-east-1 ➔ Paste Regional VPC Endpoint DNS. Click Create records. Both records are now populated in the Private Hosted Zone.
2. Configure Route 53 Resolver Forwarding Rule Configure a forwarding rule so queries from VPC On-Prem resolve against the VPC Cloud Inbound Endpoint:
In the Route 53 left navigation pane, select Inbound endpoints. Click the Inbound Endpoint and copy both assigned IPv4 addresses (e.g., 10.0.1.x and 10.0.2.x). In the navigation pane, select Resolver ➔ Rules ➔ Click Create rule. Configure Rule Parameters: Name: myS3Rule Rule type: Forward Domain name: s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com VPC: Select VPC On-prem. Outbound endpoint: Select VPCOnpremOutboundEndpoint. Target IP addresses: Add both Inbound Endpoint IP addresses recorded in Step 2. Click Submit. The resolver forwarding rule transitions to status Complete.
3. Validate DNS Resolution from On-Premises Host Reconnect to the Test-Interface-Endpoint EC2 instance via Session Manager. Execute DNS lookup using the dig command: dig +short s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com [!NOTE] The DNS query returns the private IP addresses belonging to the VPC Cloud interface endpoints (10.0.x.x), proving that conditional DNS forwarding functions across the VPN link.
Cross-Check with VPC Console: Inspect the Subnets tab of s3-interface-endpoint; the returned IPs match the assigned ENI private IPs exactly. Query S3 using standard regional endpoint addressing: aws s3 ls --endpoint-url https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com The bucket inventory returns immediately without errors. Type exit to close the terminal session. 4. Engineering Takeaways Pairing Route 53 Resolver with Private Hosted Zones delivers three architectural benefits:
Application Transparency: On-premises applications require zero SDK code adjustments or hardcoded endpoint overrides. Resilience & High Availability: DNS automatically round-robins across multiple Availability Zone ENIs. End-to-End Privacy: 100% of network traffic travels across the IPsec VPN tunnel and AWS private backbone.

title: Access Control with VPC Endpoint Policies
content:
Technical Objective By default, VPC Endpoints ship with a Full Access policy allowing any workload in the VPC to communicate with any Amazon S3 bucket across any AWS account worldwide. In enterprise production environments, this unrestricted access creates a data exfiltration risk if an internal actor or compromised instance attempts to offload corporate intellectual property into an external bucket.
A VPC Endpoint Policy is a resource-based policy attached directly to the endpoint that functions as an infrastructure-level perimeter guardrail, restricting data transfers exclusively to explicitly authorized corporate S3 buckets.
1. Baseline Verification & Creating a Second S3 Bucket Open the Session Manager console session on Test-Gateway-Endpoint. Query the initial bucket created in step 5.3: aws s3 ls s3://<your-first-bucket-name> The 1GB testfile.xyz object returns successfully. Create a second S3 Bucket: In the S3 Management Console, click Create bucket. Bucket name: Follow your existing naming scheme appended with -2 (e.g., fcj-hybrid-s3-test-<your-name>-2). Leave other settings at default values and click Create bucket. 2. Apply Custom Restriction on Gateway Endpoint Policy Open the Amazon VPC Console ➔ Select Endpoints ➔ Select s3-gwe. Select the Policy tab ➔ Click Edit policy ➔ Select Custom. Paste the following JSON policy (replace <yourbucketname-2> with your second bucket name): { "Id": "Policy1631305502445", "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "RestrictAccessToSpecificBucketOnly", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": "*", "Action": "s3:*", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::<yourbucketname-2>", "arn:aws:s3:::<yourbucketname-2>/*" ] } ] } Click Save changes. The perimeter restriction takes effect immediately. 3. Empirical Security Testing In the Test-Gateway-Endpoint terminal session, attempt to query the first bucket again: aws s3 ls s3://<your-first-bucket-name> Result: The command fails immediately with: An error occurred (AccessDenied) when calling the ListObjectsV2 operation: Access Denied. Create a second 1GB test file and upload it to the whitelisted second bucket: cd ~ fallocate -l 1G test-bucket2.xyz aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-2nd-bucket-name> Result: The transfer completes successfully at full speed. Attempt to upload the same file into the unauthorized first bucket: aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-1st-bucket-name> Result: Operation rejected with an immediate AccessDenied error. 4. Security Engineering Takeaway This experiment demonstrates that VPC Endpoint Policies evaluate requests as an independent authorization boundary. Even if the EC2 instance role possesses unrestricted AdministratorAccess, any API call traversing the VPC endpoint that targets a non-whitelisted resource is denied at the network layer. This provides an effective guardrail against accidental or malicious data exfiltration.

title: Workshop
content:
Secure Hybrid Access to Amazon S3 via VPC Endpoints Architecture Objectives In hybrid cloud production environments, routing data transfers between on-premises datacenters and Amazon S3 over the public internet introduces unnecessary latency, compliance risks, and data exposure. This workshop deploys a zero-trust network routing solution using two types of VPC Endpoints:
Gateway VPC Endpoint (AWS VPC Workloads): Routes traffic from EC2 instances to Amazon S3 directly using VPC route tables, requiring zero public IP assignment, NAT Gateway, or Internet Gateway (IGW). Interface VPC Endpoint / AWS PrivateLink (On-Premises Workloads): Provisions dedicated private IP addresses (Elastic Network Interfaces - ENIs) inside the VPC, enabling on-premises servers to communicate with S3 over an IPsec Site-to-Site VPN tunnel or AWS Direct Connect. [On-Premises Data Center] │ (IPsec VPN / Direct Connect) ▼ [AWS Transit Gateway] ▼ [Interface Endpoint (ENI Private IP)] ────(AWS PrivateLink)────► [Amazon S3] ▲ [Cloud VPC EC2] ─────(Route Table: Gateway Endpoint)─────────────────┘ Workshop Roadmap 5.1 Workshop Overview & Topology — Dual-VPC architecture connecting Cloud VPC and simulated On-Premises VPC. 5.2 Prerequisites & Environment Provisioning — Deploy base infrastructure via AWS CloudFormation and configure IAM policies. 5.3 Accessing S3 from VPC via Gateway Endpoint — Configure prefix list route tables and verify private 1GB payload transfers with AWS Systems Manager. 5.4 Accessing S3 from On-Premises via Interface Endpoint — Configure StrongSwan VPN routing, Interface Endpoints, and Route 53 Resolver conditional DNS forwarding. 5.5 Restricting Access with VPC Endpoint Policies — Apply resource-level IAM policies to restrict endpoint access strictly to designated buckets. 5.6 Resource Cleanup & Cost Governance — De-provision Private Hosted Zones, Resolver rules, endpoints, and CloudFormation stacks to avoid recurring idle costs.

title: Resource Teardown & Cost Governance
content:
Resource De-provisioning Procedure To prevent recurring hourly charges from idle resources—particularly Interface Endpoints, Route 53 Resolver Endpoints, Transit Gateway attachments, and StrongSwan VPN EC2 instances—execute teardown following strict dependency order:
1. Delete Route 53 Private Hosted Zone & Resolver Rules Open the Amazon Route 53 Management Console ➔ Navigate to Hosted zones. Select the Private Hosted Zone s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com ➔ Click Delete ➔ Type delete to confirm. In the left navigation pane, select Resolver ➔ Rules. Select rule myS3Rule ➔ Click Disassociate to detach it from VPC On-prem ➔ Click Delete to permanently remove the rule. 2. Delete Manually Created VPC Endpoints Open the Amazon VPC Management Console ➔ Select Endpoints. Select both endpoints created during the workshop: s3-gwe (Gateway Endpoint) s3-interface-endpoint (Interface Endpoint) Click Actions ➔ Select Delete VPC endpoints ➔ Type delete to confirm. 3. Empty and Delete Test S3 Buckets Open the Amazon S3 Management Console. Select each test bucket (fcj-hybrid-s3-test-... and fcj-hybrid-s3-test-...-2). Click Empty ➔ Type permanently delete to erase the uploaded 1GB test payloads. Once emptied, click Delete ➔ Type the bucket name to confirm deletion. 4. Delete CloudFormation Stacks Open the AWS CloudFormation Management Console in region us-east-1. Select and initiate deletion for the two stacks in sequence: PLOnpremSetup (Resolver endpoints and simulated on-premises DNS) PLCloudSetup (Cloud VPC, Transit Gateway, and EC2 instances) Wait approximately 5-10 minutes for CloudFormation to fully de-provision all VPCs, subnets, route tables, and release associated Elastic IP addresses.
5. AWS CloudFormation (Part 1): Template Anatomy & Stack Provisioning What did we learn today? Anatomy of a Production CloudFormation Template: Mastered the standard declarative YAML sections: AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09', Description, Parameters (accepting runtime variables such as CIDR blocks and environment tiers), Mappings (region-to-AMI lookups), Conditions (conditional resource activation), Resources (mandatory cloud primitives), and Outputs (cross-stack reference exports). Mastery of Intrinsic Functions: !Ref: Referencing user parameters or extracting physical resource IDs. !Sub: Dynamic variable string interpolation (e.g., ${AWS::StackName}-public-subnet-1). !GetAtt: Deep attribute extraction (e.g., !GetAtt MyVPC.Arn or !GetAtt MyEC2.PrivateIp). !Join: Concatenating strings with specific delimiters. Hands-on Network Stack Provisioning: Authored a 180-line network-foundation.yaml template declaring an isolated VPC (10.0.0.0/16), Internet Gateway, 2 Public Subnets, 2 Private Subnets, Route Tables, and Route Table Associations. Root cause: Inconsistent white-space indentation under Properties blocks. Solution: Integrated cfn-lint and the VS Code CloudFormation extension to lint templates prior to CLI execution. Circular Dependency Hangs: When declaring an Internet Gateway attachment alongside route creation, the default route failed because the IGW was not fully attached. Solution: Added an explicit DependsOn: AttachGateway directive on the AWS::EC2::Route resource. 📌 Tuesday (11/03/2026) - AWS CloudFormation (Part 2): Nested Stacks, Change Sets & Drift Detection What did we learn today? Modular Architecture with Nested Stacks: Overcame single-template resource limits and enforced separation of concerns by creating a Root Stack (master.yaml) that references three S3-staged child templates: network-stack.yaml, database-stack.yaml (RDS), and compute-stack.yaml (EC2 & ALB) using AWS::CloudFormation::Stack. Safe Deployment with Change Sets: Avoided direct in-place updates on production stacks. Change Sets allow visual pre-flight inspection of additions (Add), modifications (Modify), and deletions (Remove), specifically highlighting potential stateful replacements (Replacement: True/False). Configuration Auditing with Drift Detection: Mastered the Drift Detection engine to verify live AWS resource configurations against the template state, immediately spotting unmanaged manual changes (such as rogue security group inbound rules added via console). Accidental Deletion Protection: Enabled Termination Protection on critical stacks, preventing human error from deleting production infrastructure. Encountered Challenges & Solutions: Handling the UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED State: An incompatible DB subnet group modification caused stack rollback to fail, locking the stack in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED. Solution: Inspected CloudFormation Stack Events, triggered Continue Update Rollback with Skip Resources on the stuck resource, restoring the stack to UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE. 📌 Wednesday (11/04/2026) - Modern Software-Defined Infrastructure with AWS CDK What did we learn today? Software-Defined Cloud Engineering: Replaced lengthy declarative templates with TypeScript, applying Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) paradigms, compile-time type safety, automated code completion (IntelliSense), and unit testing frameworks. Construct Abstraction Levels: Level 1 (L1 - Cfn Resources): 1-to-1 direct mapping to CloudFormation resource types (e.g., CfnVPC). Level 2 (L2 - AWS Managed): Opinionated AWS best-practice constructs that configure subnets, route tables, and security groups with sensible defaults in minimal code lines (e.g., new ec2.Vpc(this, 'MyVpc', { maxAzs: 2 })). Level 3 (L3 - Architectural Patterns): Multi-service composite patterns (e.g., ApplicationLoadBalancedFargateService). Solution: Executed cdk bootstrap once for the target account/region to provision the CDKToolkit assets stack. Library Version Mismatches: Encountered dependency conflicts between legacy @aws-cdk packages and the consolidated aws-cdk-lib. Solution: Standardized the package manifest to AWS CDK v2 with exclusive references to aws-cdk-lib. 📌 Thursday (11/05/2026) - Centralized Fleet Operations via Systems Manager & AWS Backup What did we learn today? Secure Secrets Management via SSM Parameter Store: Stored database connection strings and API credentials as SecureString parameters encrypted with AWS KMS, allowing applications to retrieve runtime credentials securely without hardcoding secrets in configuration files. Centralized Data Protection with AWS Backup: Configured an immutable Backup Vault protected by Vault Lock (WORM compliance), preventing snapshot deletion even by the AWS account root user. Configured an automated daily Backup Plan for EBS and RDS with a 30-day retention cycle. Root cause: Missing the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore IAM role, and the private subnet lacked either an internet NAT gateway or VPC Interface Endpoints for SSM (ssm, ssmmessages, ec2messages). Solution: Attached the instance profile and provisioned VPC Endpoints for private SSM communication. 📌 Friday (11/06/2026) - Week 8 Review, Worklog Finalization & Capstone Project Development What did we learn today?
